The Legal Pad

A legal pad on a kitchen table can make a hard decision look like arithmetic. Two columns. A coffee ring in the corner. One age on the left, another on the right. The numbers matter. They are not the whole decision.

I’ve sat at that table more than once, with someone I love, trying to turn a life decision into a number we could both live with. It never quite works that way. Every answer on that pad depends on things the pad can’t hold — how much income you need now, what happens to the person left behind, how much certainty is worth compared to how much money.

I tell you that because I don’t want you to think this book is going to hand you a single correct age. It isn’t. Social Security’s claiming rules will tell you exactly what each age does to the number on your check. They will not tell you what to do with your one life, and neither will I.

Two questions, before any of the rules

I taught civics for 34 years in a Cumberland County high school, which means I spent three decades untangling fine print for teenagers who didn’t want to hear it. That habit didn’t retire when I did. So before we get into full retirement age, spousal rules, the earnings test or any of it, let me put two questions on the board, because every answer in this book runs through them.

  1. What do you need this money for, starting the month you claim it?
  2. If you go first, or your spouse does, what happens to the survivor’s check?

The first question is about your own finances today: can you cover your bills without claiming, or does the household need the income now? The second question is about the person left behind, and it’s the one I’ve watched people skip, because nobody likes doing that arithmetic at a kitchen table. I’ll come back to it in Chapter 14, and I’d rather you know now that it’s coming than have it surprise you nine chapters in.

Chapter 15 separates the earnings test from the tax rules, because they are two different ways work can affect your check.

Why this book labels every number by year

Now the part I’d rather tell you on page two than have you discover on page eighty.

Every fall, the Social Security Administration announces the next year’s Cost-of-Living Adjustment, the new earnings-test limits, and the new taxable maximum — the ceiling on wages subject to Social Security tax. SSA publishes the current COLA, earnings-test limits, and taxable maximum at ssa.gov/cola. Before you file, check that page and use the figures for the year you will receive benefits. This book labels every figure by year and does not ask you to rely on a forecast.

What doesn’t move with the calendar is the structure underneath the dollars. Full retirement age is still calculated the same way it was calculated last year. The math behind an early claim or a delayed one hasn’t changed. Learn the structure here. Check the dollars at the source before you file.

Where your own numbers come from

Everything in this book is a rule. None of it is your number.

Your number lives in one place, and that place is your earnings record at the Social Security Administration. You get to it through a free my Social Security account at ssa.gov/myaccount. Set one up before you reach Chapter 10, because nearly every worksheet in this book asks you to write down something only that account can tell you.

Inside it is your Social Security Statement. SSA says the redesigned Statement shows a bar graph of your personalized retirement estimates at nine different starting ages, your earnings history, and instructions on how to report an error if you find one. SSA also says it mails a paper Statement three months before the birthday of workers 60 and older who don’t have an online account. If one of those envelopes has been arriving and going straight into a drawer, go dig it out.

Read the earnings history line by line. Not the total at the bottom. The years.

You’re looking for a year that shows nothing when you know you worked, a year that looks too small, work under a name you no longer use, or a self-employment year you filed late. Those lines feed the benefit calculation, so an error there follows you into every chapter that comes after this one. SSA’s own Statement tells you how to report one. Do it sooner rather than later: old records are harder to reconstruct, and the employer who could have confirmed a 1986 paycheck may not be in business anymore.

Once the record looks right, use SSA’s calculators rather than arithmetic of your own. The agency’s Benefit Calculators page at ssa.gov/benefits/calculators lists several, and they do different jobs. The Retirement Age Calculator tells you your full retirement age. The Early or Late Retirement Calculator shows what filing early or delaying does to the amount. The Earnings Test Calculator is for someone working while receiving benefits this year. The Benefits for Spouses Calculator handles early claiming on a spouse’s record. SSA notes that the Quick Calculator and the Online Calculator don’t access your record at all, so whatever comes out of those is only as good as what you typed into them.

Here’s my rule, and I’d ask you to adopt it. SSA supplies the numbers. This book supplies what the numbers mean. You won’t find an estimate of your monthly check anywhere in these pages, and I’d be careful with anyone who offers you one without looking at your record first.

These rules don’t sit in separate rooms

The chapters are separate. Your life isn’t.

Whether you’re married, how long you were married to someone you’re no longer married to, whether you’re still working, and whether you expect to outlive your spouse or be outlived by them — those facts reach across the chapter divisions and change each other’s answers. A decision that looks right when you read Chapter 10 on its own can look different after Chapter 14.

Three places where that happens, so you’ll recognize them when they arrive. The age you claim your own retirement benefit can affect what a surviving spouse receives later, which is why Chapter 14 exists and why I asked you the survivor question up front. Work before full retirement age interacts with what SSA actually pays you in those months, covered in Chapter 15, and separately with how much of your benefit gets taxed, covered in Chapter 16. And a marriage that ended in divorce can still matter to your benefit, under rules that differ depending on whether your ex-spouse is living or has died, which is why Chapters 13 and 14 are two chapters instead of one.

Those crossings are the reason I’d ask you to read every chapter that touches your situation before you settle on an age, not after.

One piece of this book you won’t find restated in full

If you’ve also got a Medicare decision ahead of you, that’s the subject of a companion book, Medicare Made Plain, not this one. I mention it once, here, because the two programs get tangled together in people’s minds and the rules are not the same. I’d rather give you one full book than half-cover a second program inside this one. This book stays on Social Security: when to claim, what spouses and survivors are owed, what work and taxes do to the number, and what the repeal of two old pension-offset rules means if it applies to you.

The order these chapters follow

Claiming Social Security isn’t one decision wearing different hats. It’s a sequence, and I’ve arranged the chapters the way a real person actually runs into these questions, not the order a glossary would put them in.

We start with full retirement age and the claiming range from 62 to 70, because every other chapter leans on that one. Then the breakeven question, and why it’s a starting point for your thinking and not an answer by itself. Then spousal benefits, then the separate and stricter rules for a divorced spouse.

Then survivor and divorced-survivor benefits, which carry their own age table and their own full retirement age — one that isn’t always the age you’d expect. Then we cover work before full retirement age and the later recalculation for months benefits were withheld. It is not an immediate dollar-for-dollar refund. Then the Cost-of-Living Adjustment and how your benefit gets taxed. People often fold those two into one mechanism. They aren’t.

Then the Social Security Fairness Act, which repealed two rules that used to cut benefits for people with a pension from work that didn’t pay into Social Security — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset. Teaching careers were among the jobs affected. If you or your spouse spent years in one of those jobs, that chapter is worth reading.

Every chapter that deals with a real decision ends with a worksheet or a checklist built to be written on, not admired. Chapter 90 lists every figure this book used, with its source and its year. Chapter 99 is short, on purpose, because by then you won’t need another summary from me — you’ll need to go set up your own my Social Security account and look at your actual numbers instead of mine.

When to put the book down and call someone

I taught school. I am not a financial planner, a tax preparer, or a benefits counselor, and I’d think less of myself for pretending otherwise. Most of what’s in here you can handle with a pencil and an afternoon. Some of it you shouldn’t.

Call SSA directly at 1-800-772-1213, or make an appointment at an office, when the problem is your record rather than your decision. A missing or wrong year of earnings. A name change that never caught up with your file. A question about whether a particular job paid into Social Security. Anything about an ex-spouse’s or a late spouse’s record that you can’t verify yourself. SSA is the only office that can see those files and the only one that can fix them. Nobody else’s spreadsheet can.

Bring in a paid professional when the decision has a survivor in it, a non-covered pension, or a tax year that’s already crowded. By professional I mean a CPA, or a fee-only financial planner who charges you for advice rather than for a product.

Four situations that qualify. One spouse is in poor health, and the claiming order will set what the other one lives on for years. You or your spouse earned a pension from a job outside the Social Security system. Your claim lands in the same year as a large retirement-account withdrawal or the sale of a house. Or you’re already widowed and choosing between a survivor benefit and your own.

The reason isn’t that the rules are too hard to read. It’s that those decisions are hard to undo. A survivor benefit calculated from a claim made years earlier doesn’t care how reasonable the claim looked at the time.

Ask what the advice costs before you take it. And be careful with free advice from anyone who earns a commission on what you do next.

What this book won’t do

This book gives you the rules and the questions. SSA still has to confirm your own record.

No single age is right for everyone. No rule is fixed forever either. Congress proves that from time to time, most recently with the Social Security Fairness Act’s repeal of two pension-offset rules; Chapter 17 covers that repeal and tells you where to check SSA’s current implementation information.

What this book will do is put the rules in the order you’ll meet them, label each figure with its year, and tell you when to confirm the current amount at SSA before acting. Whatever age you land on, you’ll land on it on purpose, with the numbers in front of you, instead of by accident, or by whatever your brother-in-law heard somewhere.

Get a pencil. The legal pad part is next.

Chapter 10: Full Retirement Age Isn’t 65

More people say this to me than any other sentence about Social Security: “I’ll take mine at 65.”

They say it the way you’d state your own address. No hedging. And for a long stretch of American life they’d have been right, because 65 was the age the program used for an unreduced retirement benefit, and 65 is still the age people picture when they picture retiring.

Then Congress moved it, and most of the country never got the memo.

Your full retirement age is the age at which Social Security will pay you the whole benefit your earnings record has built. Not a dollar more, not a dollar less. Claim before it and the monthly amount drops by a set percentage. Claim after it and the amount climbs by a set percentage.

For your own retirement benefit, age-based reductions and delayed credits are measured from retirement full retirement age. Survivor benefits use a separate full retirement age, covered in Chapter 14, and the timing rules for family benefits don’t simply copy the retirement rules either. So when I say “full retirement age” in this chapter and the next, I mean the retirement one, on your own record, and nothing else.

That date is probably not your 65th birthday. So we start here.

Where 65 went

SSA says it plainly on its Retirement Age Calculator page: full retirement age, also called normal retirement age, was 65 for many years, and in 1983 Congress passed a law to gradually raise it because people are living longer and are generally healthier in older age. The increase began with people born in 1938, paused at 66 for those born from 1943 through 1954, then rose again to 67 for people born in 1960 or later.

The slow laws are the ones nobody argues about. A change that lands all at once gets protests. A change that arrives two months at a time can remain unnoticed for decades.

Two things did not change in 1983, and both matter to you.

The first: 62 is still the earliest month you can start a retirement benefit. SSA states on that same page that the earliest age for retirement benefits remains 62. The second: 65 is still the Medicare age, which is the real reason the old number keeps its grip on people. That is a different program on a different clock, and this book stays on Social Security.

Two separate programs. Two separate ages. One birthday that used to cover both.

Find yours before you read another page

Here is the table from SSA’s “Starting Your Retirement Benefits Early” page, which is the official list and the one I’d want you reading over my shoulder. Find your birth year.

  • Born 1943 through 1954: full retirement age 66
  • Born 1955: 66 and 2 months
  • Born 1956: 66 and 4 months
  • Born 1957: 66 and 6 months
  • Born 1958: 66 and 8 months
  • Born 1959: 66 and 10 months
  • Born 1960 or later: 67

Write it down. Not the year — the year and the months, because those months are real money and I’ve watched people round them away.

Two wrinkles from SSA’s own footnotes, and they catch people.

If you were born on January 1 of any year, SSA figures your full retirement age using the previous year. Someone born on New Year’s Day 1960 is treated as a 1959 birth, so their full retirement age is 66 and 10 months, not 67. A hair’s difference in the hospital, two months’ difference in the rule.

And if you were born on the first of any month, SSA figures your benefit and your full retirement age as though your birthday fell in the previous month. There’s also an administrative rule worth knowing: SSA says you must be at least 62 for an entire month to receive benefits. For most birth dates, that means the first possible benefit month begins after your 62nd birthday month, so use SSA’s calculator for your exact date rather than counting on the birthday itself.

If your birth date sits on one of those boundaries, or if the date in SSA’s file isn’t the date on your birth certificate, call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 and get it settled before you plan around a number. That is a records question, and SSA is the only office that can answer it.

What claiming at 62 costs, for good

Now the part that gets glossed over in every kitchen-table conversation I’ve been part of.

An early-claim reduction is usually lasting for the months you actually get paid. It is not a temporary discount that quietly catches up at full retirement age. Later chapters cover the limited exceptions, including credit for months withheld under the earnings test, withdrawing an application within SSA’s deadline, and voluntary suspension after full retirement age. None of those is a general escape hatch, and the plain assumption to plan on is that the reduction stays. Your benefit will still get cost-of-living adjustments, which I cover in Chapter 16, but those adjustments apply to the reduced amount for as long as you draw the benefit.

Here’s what SSA’s chart shows a worker loses at 62, by birth year, against the full amount:

  • Full retirement age 66 (born 1943-1954): about 25 percent less
  • 66 and 2 months (1955): about 25.83 percent less
  • 66 and 4 months (1956): about 26.67 percent less
  • 66 and 6 months (1957): about 27.50 percent less
  • 66 and 8 months (1958): about 28.33 percent less
  • 66 and 10 months (1959): about 29.17 percent less
  • 67 (1960 or later): about 30 percent less

SSA notes those percentages are approximate due to rounding, and I’d take the agency at its word rather than treating the third decimal place as gospel.

Put a number on it, since percentages slide off the page. SSA illustrates its chart with a $1,000 monthly benefit at full retirement age. A worker whose full retirement age is 67, claiming at 62, gets $700 of that $1,000. Not $700 for a while. $700, plus whatever the cost-of-living adjustments add on top of $700, for the rest of their life. And in some situations for the rest of a surviving spouse’s life, which is why Chapter 14 exists.

Notice how little the loss varies. Whether you were born in 1952 or 1962, filing at 62 costs you somewhere between a quarter and a third of the monthly check. The reason is mechanical: the reduction is applied per month of early claiming, so as full retirement age rose, the number of early months rose with it. SSA’s chart counts 48 months between 62 and a full retirement age of 66, and 60 months between 62 and 67.

The reduction is mechanical; paying in for forty years does not change the percentage.

What waiting buys

Past your full retirement age, the arithmetic runs the other direction, and this is the part of the program I find genuinely generous.

SSA calls them delayed retirement credits. For anyone born in 1943 or later, the credit is 8 percent per year, or two-thirds of 1 percent for each month you delay beyond full retirement age. The increase stops at 70. Not “mostly stops.” Stops. No additional delayed credit accrues after 70, and filing later than 70 can forfeit months beyond SSA’s limited retroactive window.

So the full span of the decision, for someone with a full retirement age of 67, runs from about 70 percent of their full benefit at 62 to 124 percent at 70. The 70-year-old’s check is roughly three-quarters larger than the 62-year-old’s, on the same earnings record, for no reason other than the month the paperwork went in.

Three practical notes SSA publishes that tend to surface only after someone has already filed.

If you start benefits after full retirement age but before 70, some of your delayed retirement credits won’t show up right away. SSA’s example: a person whose full retirement age is 67 files at 69. The initial amount reflects credits earned through the year before that 69th birthday. Those credits raise the ongoing amount effective the following January. Don’t assume SSA will issue back pay at the higher rate for the earlier months, and don’t be alarmed when the first deposit looks smaller than the arithmetic promised.

Second, once you’ve reached full retirement age, SSA may allow up to six months of retroactivity, never for a month before full retirement age and never more than six months back. That sounds like a free gift if you’ve been slow with the paperwork. It isn’t. Before age 70, choosing those retroactive months permanently lowers the ongoing amount, because months you’re paid for are months that earn no delayed credit. Ask SSA to compare both choices, the lump sum and the later start date, before you elect anything.

Third, the personalized Retirement Calculator inside your my Social Security account will show you estimates at different start dates with credits applied, which is a cleaner way to compare ages than doing the January math yourself.

It’s a range, not a switch

Sixty-two or seventy. That’s how the conversation usually gets framed, and the framing is wrong.

You can start a retirement benefit in any month from 62 through 70. The reduction and the credit are both calculated monthly, so each month you wait moves the number: two-thirds of 1 percent per month past full retirement age, a smaller fraction per month before it. There is no cliff on a birthday. There is a slope, and you can step off it anywhere.

Which means the real question is narrower and more answerable than “when should I claim.” It’s “what would it take to wait three more months,” and then three more after that. I’ve seen people who couldn’t contemplate waiting eight years find that waiting fourteen months was entirely doable once they looked at what it bought.

The standard advice runs to extremes in both directions, and I think both extremes are badly served. “Take it as soon as you can, before the money runs out” treats a lifetime inflation-adjusted benefit as though it were a bank balance someone might repossess. “Always wait until 70” ignores people in poor health, people with no other income, and people whose spouse’s record changes the math entirely. Neither slogan has met you.

What I’d ask you to hold onto from this chapter is smaller and harder to argue with. Nearly every month between 62 and 70 is a possible starting month, and each one carries a known price. That price list is published by the agency that will cut the check.

Your claiming-range worksheet

Pull out the pad. This takes ten minutes and it’s the foundation for every chapter after this one.

  1. Write your birth month and year. If you were born on January 1, write the previous year beside it and circle it.
  2. Write your full retirement age from the list above — the years and the months. Confirm it with SSA’s Retirement Age Calculator at ssa.gov rather than trusting my list or your memory.
  3. Write the exact calendar month and year you reach that age. This is your zero point. Example: born March 15, 1958; full retirement age 66 and 8 months; full retirement age month November 2024.
  4. Now rule four columns across the page and head them: start month, your age that month, SSA’s estimate, and the future earnings you assumed. Four columns, because the fourth one is the column people forget and then wonder why the number moved.
  5. Fill one row for age 62, one for your full retirement age month, and one for age 70, copying each dollar figure from the Retirement Calculator in your my Social Security account. That calculator asks what you expect to earn between now and your start date; enter a figure you’d actually bet on, write it in column four, and keep it the same across all your rows so the comparison is honest.
  6. Fill one more row for each of three start dates that are plausible for you — not ideal, plausible. Your earliest acceptable, your likely, and your stretch. Run each one through the calculator and copy the estimate.
  7. Now use the percentages from earlier in this chapter only as a sanity check, not as your math. If your full retirement age is 67 and the calculator says $1,000 at 67, the age-62 row should land near a 30 percent reduction, which leaves 70 percent: $1,000 times 0.70 is $700. SSA’s own chart uses exactly that example. If your own age-62 row is nowhere near that ratio, you’ve entered something wrong, or your earnings assumption changed between rows.
  8. Circle the highest and lowest dollar figures on the page. The gap between them, not the percentages, is the actual size of this decision.

Those three plausible dates are what the rest of this book works on. Chapter 11 takes the breakeven arithmetic to them. Chapters 12 through 14 show how a spouse, an ex-spouse or a survivor can move them. Chapter 15 deals with what happens if you’re still working when one of those dates arrives.

One instruction for the dollar columns, and I’ll keep repeating it: the only figure worth using is the one from your own record. An estimate from a magazine, a neighbor, or a website that never saw your earnings history is a guess wearing a dollar sign.

Go log into your account and write down the number at your full retirement age. The next chapter does something with it.

Chapter 11: The Breakeven Question

Joan had already decided. She just hadn’t told me yet.

It was a Sunday, and the legal pad was between us with my handwriting on the left side and her handwriting on the right. She was turning 62 that spring. Her position was one sentence long: she had worked since she was nineteen, she wanted the money, and she wanted it while she could still carry a suitcase up a flight of stairs.

Mine took longer to say, which should have been my first clue. I had the percentages copied out of the agency’s own pages. I had the gap between the age-62 number and the age-70 number, and the gap was large enough that I kept underlining it. I believed, with the confidence of a man who had never actually filed for anything, that we should both wait until 70.

Somewhere in the second hour she asked me the only question that mattered: “And what year does your pencil say I die?”

I didn’t have an answer. The pad didn’t either.

What a breakeven age actually is

Set the argument aside and look at the arithmetic, because the arithmetic is simple and most people have never seen it done.

A breakeven age is the age at which the total money collected from a later claim catches up with the total money collected from an earlier one. That’s the whole idea. The early claimer gets a head start of smaller checks. The later claimer gets a bigger check for fewer months. Somewhere out in the future, the running totals cross.

Finding the crossing point takes three numbers and one division.

One: the head start. Multiply the smaller monthly benefit by the number of months the early claimer collects before the later claimer starts.

Two: the monthly gap. Subtract the smaller monthly benefit from the larger one.

Three: divide the head start by the monthly gap. That gives you the number of months, counted from the later start date, that the patient claimer needs in order to catch up.

Let me put it on the board with the agency’s own illustration, the $1,000 monthly benefit at a full retirement age of 67 that I used in the last chapter. At 62 that worker’s check is $700. At 67 it’s $1,000. At 70, with three years of delayed credits at 8 percent a year, it’s $1,240.

Claiming at 62 instead of 67: the head start is 60 months of $700, which is $42,000. The monthly gap after 67 is $300. Divide $42,000 by $300 and you get 140 months, which is 11 years and 8 months past 67. The totals cross a few months before that worker’s 79th birthday.

Claiming at 67 instead of 70: the head start is 36 months of $1,000, which is $36,000. The monthly gap after 70 is $240. Divide and you get 150 months, 12 and a half years past 70. The totals cross around 82 and a half.

Claiming at 62 instead of 70, the comparison people actually argue about: the head start is 96 months of $700, or $67,200. The gap is $540 a month. Divide and you get a little over 124 months, roughly 10 years and 4 months past 70. The totals cross somewhere in the reader’s 81st year.

Three comparisons on one earnings record, and the crossing points land across a four-year spread. There is no single breakeven age for a person. There’s a breakeven age for each pair of dates you’re comparing, which is the first thing the magazine articles leave out.

What I left out of that arithmetic

Everything I just did is simplified, and I’d rather name the simplifications than let you find them later.

I left out the cost-of-living adjustment, which is applied as a percentage and therefore raises both the small check and the large one. I left out taxes, which can reach some portion of your benefit depending on your other income; that’s Chapter 16, and it’s a different mechanism from anything in this chapter. I left out the earnings test, which can hold back benefits if you claim early while still working, and which has its own recalculation later; that’s Chapter 15. I left out any return you might earn by investing the early checks instead of spending them. I left out the January timing quirk from the last chapter, where some delayed credits don’t show up in the monthly amount until the following year.

And I left out the largest variable of all, which is what a spouse’s or a survivor’s benefit does to the comparison. For a married couple, a breakeven run on one person’s record alone can point in a direction the household’s actual numbers don’t support. Chapters 12 through 14 are where that gets dealt with, and if you’re married, widowed or divorced after a long marriage, I’d ask you not to settle on an age until you’ve read them.

So treat a hand-run breakeven as a rough map, not a survey. It tells you the neighborhood. It does not tell you the lot line.

The calculator doesn’t know when you’ll die

Here’s the uncomfortable center of this whole business, and I don’t think it gets said plainly enough.

Every breakeven calculation is a bet on your own date of death. Not a prediction. A bet. If you claim late and die at 74, the early claim would have paid you more. If you claim early and live to 93, the late claim would have paid you a great deal more. The math is honest about this and the people quoting the math usually aren’t.

The agency does publish a Life Expectancy Calculator at ssa.gov, and it’s worth five minutes. But read what it says about itself: it shows the average number of additional years a person can expect to live, based only on the sex and date of birth you enter. Based only on. It doesn’t know about your blood pressure, your parents, your cigarettes, or the fact that every woman on your mother’s side made it past 90. An average is a statement about a population. You are one person, and you will not die on average.

Which means the useful version of this question isn’t actuarial, it’s personal. Your own health, honestly assessed. What your family history looks like on both sides. What your physician actually said at your last visit, as opposed to what you told your spouse your physician said. That information is yours, it’s better than any table, and it belongs in this decision more than any percentage does.

If your health is genuinely uncertain, that’s one of the cases where I’d stop reading and ask someone. Not a stranger with a spreadsheet. A fee-only financial planner or a CPA who will look at your whole picture, charge you for the hour, and tell you what the survivor-adjusted numbers look like.

The question I’d ask instead

Here’s my opinion, and it runs against most of what you’ll hear.

“When do I break even” is the wrong first question for a lot of people, because it quietly assumes the goal is to collect the most total dollars from the government before you die. That’s a reasonable goal if you’re planning an estate. It’s a strange goal if you’re planning a life.

Flip it and ask which risk you’d rather carry.

Claim early and you carry the risk of living a long time on a smaller monthly check. It’s an inflation-adjusted check that keeps arriving as long as you do, which is exactly what you want when you’re 89 and the retirement account has been drawn down for two decades. The smaller it is, the less it covers in that year.

Claim late and you carry the risk of dying before the bigger check has paid off, having spent down other savings to bridge the gap. Your heirs may inherit less. You may also spend your late sixties with less cash and more worry than you needed to.

Neither risk is the responsible one. They’re just different, and the right answer depends on which one would actually hurt your household. A person with a pension, good health and a long-lived family is carrying one kind of exposure. A person in poor health with no other savings is carrying another. Any advice that hands both of them the same age is advice that never met either of them.

The agency says this too, in its own flat way. On its page about what to consider when planning for retirement, it states there is no “best age” for everyone and that the decision is yours, based on your personal situation. Then it lists six things to weigh. Are you still working. What is your life expectancy. Will you still have health insurance. Are you eligible for benefits on someone else’s record. Do you have other income to support you if you delay. Will other family members be eligible on your record. Not one of those six is a breakeven calculation. All six are facts about your life.

And one sentence on that page deserves to be read twice. “The benefit amount you first receive sets the base for the amount you will receive the rest of your life.”

How we settled it

Joan filed at 62. She has never once regretted it, and she will tell you so without being asked.

I held out. Not to 70, which is what I’d been underlining on the pad, but to 67. I’d like to tell you I arrived there through superior reasoning. What actually happened is that I ran the household numbers with her check already arriving, saw that we didn’t need mine yet, and then kept not needing it until a date arrived that I’d already decided I could live with.

The compromise was this: her money started early, which took the pressure off, and that took the pressure off me to start mine. Two decisions that looked like opposites turned out to depend on each other. If she had waited, I would almost certainly have claimed sooner, and we’d have ended up in roughly the same place by a different road.

Was 67 optimal? I don’t know. I still don’t. If I live to 95 I left money on the table, and if I’d waited to 70 and died at 72 I’d have left a different pile on a different table. What I can tell you is that we chose it in daylight, with the numbers written down, and neither of us has spent a night since wondering what the other one was thinking.

The honest outcome is a claiming age you chose with the household numbers in front of you, knowing what the arithmetic could not settle.

Your breakeven worksheet

Get out the page from the last chapter, the one with your start months, your ages, the estimates from your my Social Security account, and your assumed future earnings. You’ll do this once for each pair of dates you’re seriously weighing.

  1. Pick two rows from that page. Call the earlier one A and the later one B. Most people should run this at least twice: earliest against likely, and likely against stretch.
  2. Count the months from A’s start month to B’s start month. Write the count.
  3. Multiply A’s monthly estimate by that month count. That’s the head start, in dollars. Write it down and look at it for a second, because it’s a real number and people who favor waiting tend to wave it away.
  4. Subtract A’s monthly estimate from B’s. That’s the monthly gap.
  5. Divide line 3 by line 4. The answer is in months. Divide by 12 if you want years.
  6. Add that span to B’s start age. That’s your breakeven age for this pair of dates. Circle it.
  7. Repeat for your other pair. Notice that the two answers are different ages, and that neither one is “your breakeven.”
  8. Now write one more line at the bottom of the page: the age you’d have to reach for waiting to have been worth it, and your honest guess at whether you’ll get there.

Keep the arithmetic in today’s dollars and don’t try to adjust for inflation by hand. You’ll introduce more error than you remove. Use your my Social Security estimates as inputs. For taxes, ask a qualified tax professional; for household cash-flow and survivor scenarios, use a fiduciary fee-only planner with Social Security experience, and confirm benefit-entitlement questions with SSA.

What the page can’t tell you

Before you act on any circled age, run down this list. If you answer yes to any of the first four, do not use this simple breakeven age by itself. Apply the relevant rules in Chapters 12-15, then compare the revised household scenarios.

  • Do you need the income now to cover ordinary bills, without borrowing or selling something you’d rather keep?
  • Is there a health condition, in you or your spouse, that a reasonable person would weigh here?
  • Does a current spouse, a late spouse or a ten-year marriage that ended in divorce figure in your situation? If so, Chapters 12 through 14 can move your answer, and the survivor question in particular can move it a long way.
  • Will you be working between now and the date you’re considering? Chapter 15 covers what that does.
  • Do you have other income or savings that could carry the household while you delay, and have you checked what drawing them down actually costs you?
  • Would the larger check at an older age change how you’d live at 85, or would it just be a larger number?

Six questions, and a breakeven calculator can’t answer a single one of them. That’s not a failure of the calculator. It’s a statement about what kind of decision this is.

Joan’s pencil question is still the best one anybody’s asked me about Social Security, and I’ve never been able to answer it. What I could do, eventually, was stop pretending the pad knew something I didn’t.

Next we add a second record to the page, because a spouse’s earnings can change the household answer.

Chapter 12: The Spousal Benefit Is Not Half of Your Spouse’s Check

Add the checks each of you actually qualifies to receive. What you cannot add is your own retirement estimate and a second, full spousal check without asking SSA whether any spousal excess is payable.

A spousal benefit is not a second full retirement check, and it is not automatically half of the deposit your spouse receives. It is a benefit calculated from the worker’s record, with its own eligibility rules and its own reduction if you claim before your full retirement age. If you have a retirement benefit on your own record, SSA compares the two; it does not simply stack two whole checks.

Chapter 11 compared start dates using one worker’s estimate. Here the household has two records. That changes the questions, not the basic rule from Chapter 10: your own full retirement age still matters.

The half-benefit ceiling

The Social Security Administration says a spouse may receive up to half of the worker’s benefit amount at the worker’s full retirement age. That amount is sometimes called the worker’s primary insurance amount. It is the benchmark SSA uses for the calculation, not necessarily the check currently landing in the worker’s bank account.

The distinction matters if the worker claimed early or delayed. The ceiling is based on the worker’s full-retirement-age amount; delayed retirement credits the worker earns by waiting beyond that age do not raise the spouse’s maximum to half of the larger delayed check. SSA’s Family Benefits page describes the figure as up to half of what the family member would get at full retirement age.

“Up to” is doing useful work in that sentence. It is a ceiling, not a promise that every spouse will receive exactly half. Your age when you start, your own earnings record, and whether you meet the eligibility conditions all affect what SSA pays.

Here is a made-up example, just to show the arithmetic. Suppose the worker’s full-retirement-age amount is $2,400 a month. Half is $1,200. If the other spouse’s own full-retirement-age retirement benefit is $900, the potential spousal amount at that age is the difference: $300. The combined retirement payment would be $1,200 before any adjustments, not $900 plus a separate $1,200 check.

If that spouse’s own retirement benefit were $1,350, it would already be higher than the $1,200 spousal ceiling in this illustration. There would be no additional spousal amount to bring the total up. SSA’s Family Benefits page says that when you qualify for other Social Security benefits, it pays the highest amount you are eligible for rather than adding the full payment amounts together.

Those figures are round numbers for explaining the structure. They are not estimates for your record, and they do not account for claiming before full retirement age. For an actual comparison, use the spouse benefit calculator listed on SSA’s Benefit Calculators page or ask SSA to estimate both records.

The marriage rule, and who can qualify

For an ordinary current-spouse benefit, SSA says you may be eligible if you have been married for at least one year and are age 62 or older. There is a separate path for a spouse of any age who is caring for the worker’s child who is under 16 or has a disability. The exact conditions matter; “we’ve been together a long time” is not the same as meeting SSA’s marriage and family-benefit rules.

The worker must also be entitled to retirement benefits for a standard retirement-based spousal benefit to be paid on that record. In practical terms, the worker has to apply and become entitled first. If your spouse has not filed, you generally cannot start a current-spouse retirement benefit on that record just because your own claiming age has arrived.

That order can be frustrating for a couple where one person is ready to claim and the other wants to delay. It does not mean the lower-earning spouse must claim their own retirement benefit immediately. It means you should compare the choices using both estimates and understand which benefit, if any, is available before the worker files.

There are exceptions and details that can change the answer, especially when a spouse is caring for a child or has a disability. SSA’s “Who Can Get Family Benefits” page lays out the categories, but it cannot resolve a missing date or a disputed earnings record. If your marriage history, the worker’s entitlement, or a child’s status makes the case less ordinary, contact SSA and ask for an eligibility determination before you build a household budget around the benefit.

Claiming early changes your side of the calculation

The worker’s full-retirement-age amount sets the maximum. Your own age when you apply determines how much of that maximum you can receive.

SSA’s retirement-age chart shows a spouse’s reduced percentages separately from the worker’s retirement percentages. Claiming a spousal benefit before your own full retirement age reduces it. The reduction depends on how many months early you start and on your full retirement age. It is not calculated by taking your spouse’s reduced check and cutting that in half.

The same SSA chart makes the difference visible for someone born in 1960 or later, whose full retirement age is 67. At 62, the worker’s own benefit is shown as 70 percent of the full-retirement-age amount; the spouse’s benefit is shown as 32.5 percent of the worker’s full-retirement-age amount. At 67, those examples reach 100 percent and 50 percent, respectively. Those are chart examples for that birth group, not universal percentages. If your birth year differs, use the row SSA gives you rather than borrowing the 32.5 figure.

Return to the made-up $2,400 worker example. Half is $1,200 at the spouse’s full retirement age. The $780 is the spouse-only amount at 62 for someone without an own-record benefit; if the spouse also qualifies on their own record, SSA reduces that retirement amount and any excess spousal amount separately. Ask SSA for the combined payment. It would not be $1,200 simply because the worker’s record can support that much at the spouse’s full retirement age. This illustration is only to show why both the worker’s and the spouse’s dates belong on the page; SSA must calculate the amount for your record and start month.

Use the right person’s age in the right column. The worker’s age determines the worker’s full-retirement-age amount. Your age determines the reduction on the spousal benefit. If you and your spouse were born in different years, you may have different full retirement ages; the chart in Chapter 10 is for your own retirement benefit, and SSA’s calculator can confirm the applicable dates for each of you.

Waiting until your full retirement age can matter because it avoids the early-claim reduction on the spousal portion. But waiting past full retirement age does not make the spousal maximum grow the way delayed retirement credits grow a worker’s own retirement benefit. The program treats those two amounts differently. Don’t assume that waiting to 70 turns a spousal benefit into a larger percentage of your spouse’s check. If you started your own retirement benefit early while the worker delayed filing, a later spousal supplement will not erase your earlier retirement reduction; ask SSA to compare the actual dates and both components.

The plain comparison is between the amount available on your own record, the potential spouse amount, and the month you would start. SSA can give you record-specific estimates. Your online Statement is useful for your own retirement estimate, but a spouse’s amount depends on both records and entitlement, so don’t infer it from your Statement alone.

Filing is not a menu of separate checks

People sometimes remember an old strategy: take a spousal benefit now, leave your own retirement benefit untouched, and let that one grow. Some couples could use a restricted application under earlier rules. It is not a general strategy available to everyone now.

SSA calls the modern rule “deemed filing.” If you are eligible for both your own retirement benefit and a spousal benefit, filing for one can count as filing for both. For people born on or after January 2, 1954, deemed filing generally applies when they qualify for both benefits; SSA’s filing-rules page describes the dates and exceptions. In that situation, you cannot ordinarily choose only the spousal benefit while deliberately delaying your own retirement benefit.

There are exceptions, including certain benefits connected to caring for a worker’s child and disability situations. People born before January 2, 1954 may also fall under different rules if they meet SSA’s conditions. These exceptions are specific, not a loophole to build a plan around from a headline or a neighbor’s story.

A worker’s claim date is part of the couple’s sequence, too. Since the standard spousal benefit depends on the worker being entitled, one spouse filing can make a benefit available to the other. But that does not mean the worker should file early just to unlock a payment. Compare what each person can receive on their own record, what the spousal supplement might add, and whether the worker’s decision changes future household income. Chapter 14 will address a different question: what happens to a spouse’s options after a death.

A spouse’s application does not reduce the worker’s own retirement benefit. If children or other family members may also qualify on the worker’s record, ask SSA how the family maximum applies to their payments. That is a separate calculation, and it is not a reason to guess at the spousal amount.

Two estimates, one household decision

The useful unit is not “my check” or “your check.” Put both records on the page and mark which benefit is available under each possible start date. The number that looks smaller by itself may be supplemented by a spousal amount; the larger personal benefit may mean there is no supplement at all.

If your own record is modest compared with your spouse’s, ask SSA for an estimate of the spouse amount at your full retirement age and at the month you are considering. If your own record is stronger, ask whether any excess spousal benefit is payable rather than assuming the answer from the headline figure. If the worker has not applied, ask what would become available if they did, and what that decision would do to both of your estimates.

This is also where a household cash-flow question can be mistaken for an SSA eligibility question. SSA decides whether the record and dates qualify. A fee-only financial planner can help model how different start dates affect the household’s income and savings, but cannot change SSA’s entitlement rules. If the calculation depends on an exact marriage date, a prior marriage, disability, or caring for a child, call SSA rather than asking a planner to interpret the record.

A second household, run at two start months

Figures on a page beat a rule you half-remember. So here is a second made-up household, worked at two different start months, using the early-claiming percentages SSA published on the chart from Chapter 10, as they stood when I checked in October 2026.

The higher earner has a full-retirement-age amount of $3,000. The lower earner was born in 1957, whose row on that chart sets full retirement age at 66 and 6 months, and has an own-record full-retirement-age estimate of $1,000. Both dollar figures are round for teaching. Neither is an estimate for your record.

Begin with the benchmark. Half of $3,000 is $1,500. That ceiling is set by the higher earner’s full-retirement-age amount and by nothing else. Subtract the lower earner’s own $1,000 and $500 is left. That $500 is the portion SSA would examine as a spousal supplement at the lower earner’s full retirement age, sitting on top of their own benefit. The payment to that person in that month would be around $1,500, not $1,000 plus a separate $1,500.

Now move the lower earner’s start month back to 62 and watch the two pieces move apart, because this is the step most kitchen tables get wrong.

Their own retirement benefit takes the worker reduction covering 54 early months. SSA’s 1957 row shows a $1,000 full-retirement-age benefit cut by 27.5 percent to $725 at 62. Applied to our $1,000, that leaves $725.

The $500 supplement takes a different reduction from a different column. The same 1957 row carries a 32.5 percent reduction on the spouse side, and the note under SSA’s chart says the spouse percentage is applied after the automatic halving. Take 32.5 percent off $500 and $337.50 remains. SSA’s own row prints the matching example, showing a $500 spouse’s benefit reduced to $337 for that birth year, which is the same arithmetic with the agency’s rounding. Add the two reduced pieces and this household’s lower earner is near $1,062.50 a month.

Put the two results side by side. About $1,500 at 66 and 6 months. About $1,062.50 at 62. The difference is roughly $437.50 a month, and by the rule from Chapter 10 it does not close later.

Two parts of that arithmetic deserve saying plainly.

The lower earner’s own reduction and the supplement’s reduction are different percentages drawn from different columns of the same row. Borrowing the worker percentage for both is the fastest way to build an estimate that is too high, and the error survives because the result still looks like a sensible number.

The higher earner’s start month does not move the $1,500 benchmark at all. It moves their own check, and it governs whether the supplement is available yet, which is the entitlement point from earlier in this chapter. A higher earner who waits until 70 does not lift the benchmark to half of the larger check that waiting produces.

The order of operations

If you keep one thing from this chapter, keep the sequence.

Halve the benchmark belonging to whichever of you earned more. Subtract the lower earner’s own full-retirement-age amount. If what remains is zero or less, there is no supplement to wait for, and the lower earner is facing a plain own-record start-date choice of the kind Chapter 11 laid out. If what remains is positive, reduce the own amount and the leftover supplement separately for the lower earner’s start month, using that person’s birth-year row, then ask SSA to confirm the combined figure before either of you files anything.

That sequence also tells you which question to ask on the phone. A household with no leftover supplement should ask about start months and the earnings test. A household with a leftover supplement should ask whether any excess is payable at the proposed month and what the combined payment would be. Those are different conversations, and knowing which one you are in saves a second call.

Both households in this chapter use whole dollars and ignore the annual cost-of-living adjustment, which Chapter 16 handles. SSA also rounds, so a benefit letter can differ from hand arithmetic by a dollar or two. Rounding is not the risk in this calculation. Using the wrong column, or the wrong person’s birth year, is.

Work both start months before you call, even if you are fairly sure which one you want. The gap between them is the only part of this decision that is yours to set.

Your spousal-benefit worksheet

Use this as a request list for my Social Security and an SSA conversation, not as a substitute for SSA’s calculation.

  1. Write down both birth dates, including month and day. Confirm each person’s full retirement age using SSA’s Retirement Age Calculator.
  2. On separate lines, copy each person’s retirement estimate from their own my Social Security account for the same proposed start months. Keep the assumed future earnings consistent.
  3. Write the worker’s full-retirement-age estimate. Divide it by two to find the maximum spousal benchmark before any reduction. Label it “maximum benchmark,” not “my payment.”
  4. Write the spouse’s own estimated retirement amount at the same age. Ask SSA whether a spousal amount could supplement it, and what the estimated total would be at the spouse’s proposed start month.
  5. Note whether the worker has applied and is entitled to retirement benefits. If not, ask what timing options are available and how the worker’s claim date affects access to a current-spouse benefit.
  6. Write the marriage date and, if applicable, any relevant child-care or disability facts. If the one-year condition or an exception might apply, have SSA verify eligibility from the records.
  7. Ask whether deemed filing applies to you. Give SSA your birth date and say whether you are eligible, or may be eligible, on both your own and your spouse’s records. Do not rely on an old restricted-application example unless SSA confirms it fits your case.
  8. Record the representative’s answer, the date, and what you still need to provide. If the number changes when you correct an earnings record or a date, get the estimate again before choosing a start month.

Carry both figures to SSA before you decide which application to file: what your own record pays you, and what extra amount, if any, your spouse’s record can add on top of it. Next comes the rule for a former spouse, where the marriage is counted differently and the worker’s filing date may not control access in the same way.

Chapter 13: Ten Years, Not Nine Years and Ten Months

She came to the house on a Saturday morning with a manila envelope and a question she had already answered wrong in her head. A neighbor had given her my name and, I suspect, an inflated account of what I could do about it.

Inside the envelope was a divorce decree with a county stamp on it, and a marriage certificate that had been folded into quarters for so long the creases had gone soft. She wanted to know how much she could collect on her former husband’s record. She had been told it was half. She had a number in mind and she had told her daughter about it.

I asked for the two dates. The marriage certificate said March. The decree said January, almost ten years later. Nine years and ten months.

There is no gentle way to lay that out, so I didn’t try. I told her the agency requires a marriage that lasted at least ten years before the divorce became final, and that two months short is short. She asked whether anyone could round it. Nobody can. The Social Security Administration’s own frequently asked questions state it flatly: a divorced spouse must have been married ten years to get spouse’s benefits. The agency’s eligibility page for family benefits says the same thing from the other direction, that ex-spouses married for at least ten years may be eligible.

That is the rule, and she did not have to like it.

What I could do, and what we did for the next twenty minutes at my own kitchen counter, was go through her own earnings record, because her own retirement benefit was still there and she had been treating it as a consolation prize instead of her actual benefit. That part of the conversation ended better than it started.

How the ten years are counted

Most people who lose this do not lose it by two months. They lose it by never checking the dates at all, or by counting from the separation instead of from the decree.

It turns on two dates and nothing softer: the day the marriage began, and the day the divorce became final. Both are facts printed on paper somewhere, not judgment calls.

The agency’s Program Operations Manual System is the rulebook its own staff works from, and section RS 00202.005 states the requirement with more precision than the public pages do. A divorced spouse must be finally divorced from the worker, and must have been married to them for a period of at least ten years immediately before the date the divorce became final. The same section adds the test that actually decides cases: the requirement is met if the divorce became final on or after the tenth anniversary of the marriage.

Read that twice, because it tells you which date matters. Not the date one of you moved out. Not the date the petition was filed. Not the date you stopped wearing the ring. The date the divorce became final, which is the date on the decree your court issued.

The gap between those dates can be a year or more, and people who separated in the ninth year and finalized in the eleventh often assume they fall short when they do not. The reverse happens too. A couple separates at eight years, reaches a quick agreement, and the decree lands two months before the anniversary nobody was thinking about.

There is also a provision for marriages interrupted by a divorce and a remarriage to the same person. The POMS section says the ten-year period can still be met despite an interrupting divorce. The condition is that the remarriage took place no later than the calendar year immediately following the calendar year of the divorce. The marriage has to have been in existence in each of the ten years before the final divorce. The same section notes that someone whose last divorce fails the test may still qualify based on a ten-year period of marriage immediately before an earlier divorce.

If you married the same person twice, do not try to resolve this with a calendar and a pencil. Bring all four dates to the agency and let them apply that paragraph.

The conditions people forget

The ten years are the famous part. They are not the only part.

Section RS 00202.005 lists what a claimant must do and be. File an application. Reach age 62. Not be married. And, in the condition that quietly disqualifies a lot of people with long careers, not be entitled to a retirement or disability benefit based on a primary insurance amount that equals or exceeds one half of the worker’s primary insurance amount.

That last one is worth sitting with. Chapter 12 explained the primary insurance amount as the full-retirement-age benchmark on a record. If your own benchmark is at least half of your former spouse’s benchmark, there is no divorced-spouse entitlement for you at all. Not a smaller one. None. Your own record is already carrying you past the point where the other record could add anything.

The “not be married” condition applies to benefits on a living former spouse’s record. If you remarried and that marriage is still in place, you generally cannot collect as a divorced spouse on the earlier record. If a later marriage has ended, the answer depends on how and when, and that is a question for the agency rather than for a book. Marriage is also one of the changes the agency’s reporting page tells family-benefit recipients to call about promptly, and that page lists marriage by name. If you are receiving on an ex’s record and you are planning a wedding, make the call before the honeymoon, not after.

One rule here works in your favor

Chapter 12 told you that a current spouse generally has to wait for the worker to file. A divorced spouse has a second road, and it is the one piece of this chapter that tends to surprise people.

The ordinary path requires your former spouse to be entitled to retirement or disability benefits, which in practice means they have applied. But the POMS section also describes what it calls an independently entitled divorced spouse. That claimant’s former spouse must be fully insured and age 62 throughout the first month of entitlement, and the section says plainly that the worker need not have filed a claim. The additional requirement is that you must be finally divorced from them for at least two continuous years.

So the man who refuses to file, out of strategy or stubbornness or spite, does not hold the gate shut forever. Two continuous years past the decree, with him past 62 and fully insured, and the agency can look at the claim without him.

The section defines that two-year span tightly, counting from the day of the divorce, and gives worked examples of the first month of entitlement for decrees dated at the start of a month and mid-month. If your decree is dated near the first of a month, the month your entitlement could begin may not be the one you would guess. Ask the agency to apply the count to your date rather than estimating it.

There is a second small kindness in these rules, on the agency’s filing-rules page. During a voluntary suspension, benefits payable to a worker’s spouse are suspended along with the worker’s own. The page then names the exception: a divorced spouse can continue receiving a divorced spousal benefit even if the former spouse voluntarily suspends their retirement benefit. The claim stands on the record, not on the mood of the person who built it.

What your claim does to them

This worry can keep a person from calling: they do not want to take anything from an ex-spouse, a current spouse, or a child.

Here is the documented part. The agency’s Family benefits page describes the family maximum as a limit on how much a family can get on one record. If needed, the page says, payments for the spouse and children will be lowered to stay under it. The same page states that payments to ex-spouses do not count toward the family maximum. Your divorced-spouse payment does not crowd a current spouse or a child up against that ceiling.

The agency’s frequently asked questions put the two-way version of this simply. If you are divorced and the marriage lasted at least ten years, you may be able to get benefits on your former spouse’s record. Their frequently asked questions add the mirror image: your former spouse may be able to get benefits on yours. Both doors, same hallway.

What I will not tell you is anything about what your former spouse will be told, or what their household will conclude, because that is not in the published rules and I am not going to invent it. If that specific worry is the thing stopping you, ask the agency directly when you call. Ask SSA directly what it can disclose and what information it needs from you.

You will need some information about the person. The agency’s Family benefits page says to give the representative your family member’s Social Security number, and that if you do not have it, you will be asked for other information, such as their date of birth and their parents’ names. Pull together whatever you actually have before you call. If you do not have the Social Security number, tell SSA the former spouse’s name, date of birth, and parents’ names if you know them; ask what other information it needs. The parents’ names surprise people, and they are often the only thing a long-divorced claimant can actually produce.

The amount, in one paragraph

I am not going to re-teach Chapter 12 here, because the arithmetic does not change.

A divorced-spouse benefit follows the same amount rules as a current spouse’s. The same half-benefit ceiling from Chapter 12 applies, measured against your former spouse’s full-retirement-age amount. The same reduction applies if you start before your own full retirement age. And the same comparison applies against your own retirement benefit, rather than a stack of two whole checks. The agency’s filing-rules page includes a divorced spouse inside its description of deemed filing, so the restriction Chapter 12 described applies to you as well. If you are still working, the earnings limits in Chapter 15 can hold back part of what is payable. Go back to the worksheet at the end of Chapter 12 and run it with your former spouse’s record in the worker column.

When the person has died, start over

Everything in this chapter is about a living former spouse.

If your ex-spouse has died, you are in a different section of the law with different marriage-length rules, a different age floor, different percentages and different treatment of a later remarriage. Do not carry a single conclusion from this chapter into that situation. Chapter 14 handles it, and it handles it separately for exactly this reason.

Where a professional earns their fee

Most divorced-spouse questions are clerical. You need dates, and the agency needs to see them.

The place to spend money is on documents. If you cannot find your decree, the court that issued it can give you a certified copy, usually through the clerk of courts or the county prothonotary. The court that issued it can explain its current copy process, form, fee, and processing time. Fees, forms and processing times vary by state and by county, so look up your own court’s website rather than assuming it works the way a neighbor’s did. If your marriage or divorce happened in another country, or if there was an annulment, or if the decree is unclear about when it became final, that is worth an hour with a family-law attorney licensed in the state where it was entered. A lawyer can tell you what the document legally says. Only the agency can tell you whether it satisfies RS 00202.005.

Call the agency at 1-800-772-1213 for the eligibility question itself. If the household cash-flow question underneath it is large, a fee-only planner can model the timing, but no planner can change what the decree says.

A practice file with two different clocks

Put a blank sheet beside your decree. At the top, write “marriage duration.” Farther down, write “time since divorce.” Leave space between them. Those are separate tests, and passing the first does not tell you when the second ends.

Here is a hypothetical practice file for a claim considered in 2026, not another person from my kitchen counter. The marriage began August 13, 2014. The divorce became final August 13, 2024. The claimant remains unmarried and was born May 14, 1962. The living former spouse was born June 9, 1960, is fully insured, and has not applied for retirement benefits. Assume SSA confirms that the claimant’s own primary insurance amount is below the entitlement ceiling described earlier.

On the marriage-duration line, write August 13, 2024 as the tenth anniversary. The decree landed that very day. Under SSA’s POMS RS 00202.005, checked October 4, 2026, that meets the marriage-duration requirement. A separation in November 2022 would not change this result. Keep that separation date out of the anniversary calculation.

The worker has not filed, so this file needs the independent-entitlement route. Both people are already past their sixty-second birthdays throughout the months being considered. The remaining calendar question is the continuous period since the final decree, not the length of the marriage that preceded it.

For the August 13, 2024 decree, the two-year period runs from August 13, 2024 through August 12, 2026. September 2026 is the first possible entitlement month under this route, assuming the application and all other requirements are satisfied. August is not the answer merely because the anniversary occurs in August.

That result follows the August 13 example SSA prints in RS 00202.005. Its published example uses a 2010 divorce and September 2012 entitlement; this practice file moves the same calendar pattern to 2024 and 2026. The dates here are illustrative. They are not a forecast of an actual claim’s approval.

Now try a second hypothetical file. The marriage began August 1, 2014 and the final decree is dated August 1, 2024. Keep the ages, unmarried status, insured status and benchmark assumption unchanged. Again the marriage reaches its tenth anniversary. But the divorce-duration period now runs August 1, 2024 through July 31, 2026. August 2026 becomes the first possible entitlement month. SSA’s first-day-of-the-month example supports that result.

Change only that second decree to August 2, 2024. The marriage still clears its duration test. The continuous divorce period instead ends August 1, 2026, and the first possible entitlement month moves to September 2026. RS 00202.005 prints this second-day pattern too. One day can change the earliest month without changing whether the marriage qualifies.

Do not turn either earliest month into a recommendation to claim then. These hypothetical claimants are below their full retirement age. The amount comparison belongs on Chapter 12’s worksheet; the calendar here only identifies when this particular route can open.

Give each answer somewhere to go

Beside each numbered line of the checklist below, leave a margin for one of four labels: “documented,” “SSA confirmed,” “missing,” or “does not qualify.” A certificate can document a date. It cannot confirm the former spouse’s insured status or settle the comparison between earnings records.

If the marriage-duration test fails and there is no interrupted-marriage or earlier-divorce provision to examine, stop calculating an independent-entitlement month for that marriage. Work with your own record instead. If the dates qualify but the worker has not filed, use the separate divorce-duration line. If the worker is already entitled, ask SSA about the ordinary route; the independent route’s waiting period is not a universal wait imposed on every divorced claimant.

For an unanswered line, write exactly what is missing rather than supplying a plausible answer. “I don’t know whether my former spouse filed” is usable information. “They probably filed at sixty-two” is a guess wearing a date.

You can make the request this plainly: “My decree became final on this date. My former spouse is living, and I don’t know whether they are entitled. Please check which divorced-spouse route applies and the first month I could qualify. What evidence is still needed?”

Write the answer beside the relevant line, not across the whole page as a broad “yes.” You need to know which condition was confirmed before choosing a filing month.

Your ten-year count

Do this before you call, and do it with the actual paper in front of you rather than from memory.

  1. Find the marriage certificate. Write the date exactly as it appears, month, day and year. If you cannot find it, request a copy from the vital records office in the state where you married.
  2. Find the divorce decree. Write the date the divorce became final, as the decree states it, not the date you filed and not the date you separated.
  3. Count from the marriage date to the tenth anniversary of that date. Write that anniversary on the page.
  4. Compare the anniversary with the decree date. If the decree date falls on or after the anniversary, the ten-year requirement is met. If it falls before, it is not, and no amount of explaining will move it.
  5. If you married the same person more than once, list every marriage and divorce date in order and bring the whole list. The interruption provision and the prior-divorce provision both exist, and both depend on the sequence.
  6. Write your current marital status and the date of any later marriage and its end, if it ended.
  7. Write your own full-retirement-age estimate from your my Social Security account. Then ask the agency to compare the two benchmarks under the entitlement condition above, since that comparison alone can end the question.
  8. Gather what you have on your former spouse: Social Security number if you have it, otherwise date of birth and parents’ names.
  9. Note whether they have filed for benefits, if you know, and whether the decree is at least two years old, so the agency can tell you which path applies.
  10. Write down the date you called, the representative’s answer, and what they asked you to send. If the answer depends on a document, do not treat it as settled until the document is in their hands.

The woman with the manila envelope filed on her own record about a year later, at her full retirement age, and she sends a Christmas card. What I remember is how carefully she had folded that certificate, as if the paper itself might be worth something someday.

Start with the two dates before you build a plan on them.

Chapter 14: When the Other Record Becomes Yours

The funeral home usually makes the call. Social Security says so on its own page about what to do when someone dies: a funeral home generally tells the agency, so you typically do not need to report the death yourself.

People hear that and assume the rest follows.

It does not. Reporting a death does not by itself establish a survivor claim, and the agency’s rulebook for widow and widower claims lists a filed application among the entitlement requirements, with only narrow exceptions. A death certificate moving through a county office does not put a check in your account. Ask the agency whether an application or an exception applies to you.

Chapter 13 dealt with a former spouse who is still living. This chapter deals with a spouse or former spouse who has died, and almost every number changes. The marriage-length rule is different. The earliest age is different. The percentages are different. What a later remarriage does to you is different. Carry nothing over.

Nine months for a spouse, ten years for an ex

Start with who the agency will even look at.

For a surviving spouse, the Social Security Administration’s survivor eligibility page states the condition plainly: you were married for at least nine months before your spouse’s death. Not ten years. Nine months. That one line resolves more second-marriage worry than any other sentence in this book.

For a surviving divorced spouse, the same page sets the bar at a decade of marriage, and it adds that some valid non-marital legal relationships may also qualify. The ten-year count works the way Chapter 13 described it, measured against the date the divorce became final, so use that counting checklist rather than redoing the arithmetic here.

Both rules have exceptions, and the agency says so in the next breath. Its eligibility page states that you might be eligible regardless of age and how long you were married, and names caring for a child of the person who died as one common example. The Program Operations Manual System, section RS 00207.001, is more specific about the nine months. It lists the duration requirement, then lists alternatives that can substitute for it, including being the parent of the worker’s child and certain adoptions that occurred during the marriage. There is also a separate agency policy section on exceptions to the nine-month rule.

Which means a short marriage ended by a death is not automatically a closed door. If your marriage lasted less than nine months and a child or an adoption is anywhere in the picture, do not decide this at your own table. Call 1-800-772-1213 and let them read RS 00207.001 against your facts.

One more thing from that same POMS section, and it is the kind of detail that only matters once in a lifetime. If the divorce was not final when the worker died, the agency notes that the claimant may qualify as the widow or widower rather than as the surviving divorced spouse. Separated is not divorced. If papers were pending when the death occurred, say so on the phone, because it may move you into the more generous category.

Sixty, not sixty-two

The living-ex rules in Chapter 13 used 62 as the floor. Survivor rules do not.

The agency’s Survivor Full Retirement Age page states that you can start getting survivor benefits as early as age 60, or 50 if you have a disability. Its eligibility page repeats the same ages from the other direction.

Two years earlier than the retirement floor, and ten years earlier than that if a disability qualifies you. For somebody widowed at 58 who assumed nothing existed until 62, that is a real difference in a hard year.

Early still costs, and the cost here is steep. I will put the percentages on the board in a moment.

A later marriage is not automatically the end

Here is where survivor rules diverge most sharply from the living-ex rules, and where I have watched people throw away money by guessing.

Chapter 13 said that claiming on a still-living ex generally requires you to be unmarried. For survivor benefits, the agency’s eligibility page states the condition differently: you did not remarry before age 60, or before 50 if you have a disability. Read that as a deadline, not a prohibition. Remarriage after age 60 generally does not bar aged survivor benefits. For remarriage at ages 50 to 59 with a disability, additional conditions apply, including when the disability and the benefit entitlement began, so confirm your exact dates with the agency before remarriage.

POMS RS 00207.001 states the entitlement condition as being unmarried, unless the marriage can be disregarded under the agency’s own policy section on remarriage, and for surviving divorced spouses it allows a remarriage that can be disregarded for entitlements after December 1983. RS 00207.003 is the section that spells out when a remarriage is disregarded, and for a claimant who remarried between 50 and 60 it asks whether they were disabled at the time of the remarriage, or already entitled as a disabled widow or widower then. The public page is shorthand. It is not a safe rule for timing a wedding. The practical point either way: a widow or widower who remarried in their sixties should ask the agency about the earlier record rather than assuming it closed.

I would not try to time a wedding around this on my own reading of a web page. If you are near 60 and considering remarriage, make the call first and get the answer applied to your dates. Months matter in this program, and this is one of the few places where a date you fully control is worth checking before you set it.

And once you are receiving, the agency’s survivor reporting page tells you to call promptly about updates such as marriage, income and custody changes. Tell them. Do not let them find out later.

Let me put it on the board

The percentages are the part people most often get wrong, usually by assuming a widow gets half of something.

The agency’s survivor amount page gives the scale directly. Payments start at 71.5 percent of the deceased’s benefit at the earliest claiming age and rise the longer you wait to apply. Its examples are over 75 percent at 61, over 80 percent at 63, and over 90 percent at 65. You can get up to 100 percent at your Full Retirement Age for survivor benefits.

One hundred percent. Not half. At survivor full retirement age the age-based reduction ends, though the amount can still be limited if the deceased worker received reduced retirement or disability benefits, so ask the agency to calculate the payable amount rather than reading 100 percent as a promise.
