What matters for now is that the measuring stick here is the deceased’s own benefit, not a fraction of it, which is why this chapter exists as its own chapter and why the spousal ceiling from Chapter 12 has no business in your calculation.

Now the trap in that last sentence.

Your Full Retirement Age for survivor benefits is its own age. The agency’s page on it says the survivor age falls between 66 and 67, and says explicitly that it is not always the same as the Full Retirement Age for retirement benefits. The same page carries a tool where you enter your birth date and it returns your survivor age.

Go enter your birth date. Do not take the age you learned in Chapter 10 and reuse it. Two different ages can belong to the same person in the same program, which is an odd piece of drafting, and nobody in Congress has apologized for it.

Children can also receive on the record, generally 75 percent of the parent’s benefit according to the same amount page, and the family maximum can lower everyone’s payments to stay under the limit. An ex-spouse sits outside that ceiling here too, the same carve-out Chapter 12 mentioned. If you are a widowed parent with minor children, ask the agency to run the household total rather than adding the percentages yourself.

What an early claim does to the survivor

Chapter 10 promised that one person’s claiming age can reach into another person’s benefit years later. This is the mechanism, and it is the strongest argument in this book for a higher earner to think hard before filing at 62.

POMS section RS 00615.320 describes a limit the agency’s staff applies when the worker who died had ever been entitled to a reduced retirement benefit or a reduced disability benefit. When the deceased ever received reduced retirement or disability benefits, the agency tests a ceiling: the larger of 82.5 percent of the death primary insurance amount, or the amount the worker would have received if alive.

That is a maximum. It is not a floor, and it is not your check. The same section applies the ceiling only when the survivor benefit, after adjustment for the family maximum and reduction for age, comes out above both of those figures. A survivor claiming early can receive less than either one. Ask the agency for the actual age-adjusted benefit instead of doing 82.5 percent on the back of an envelope.

Read that twice, because it is the whole argument for patience. If the higher earner in a couple claims early, the survivor’s ceiling can be tied to that reduced amount for the rest of their life. The agency’s own worked example in that section runs the comparison both ways and pays the larger of the two.

That is a planning fact, not a filing fact, and it belongs on the table while both people are alive. It is also a reason to be skeptical of the common advice that the lower earner’s claiming date is the only one worth agonizing over. Often it is the other way around.

There is a second entitlement condition in RS 00207.001 that works like the one-half test from Chapter 13, but with a different threshold. A widow, widower or surviving divorced spouse must not be entitled to a retirement benefit that equals or exceeds the deceased worker’s primary insurance amount. Half was the bar on a living ex’s record. Here it is the whole amount. A survivor with a strong record of their own can still have a survivor benefit available where a divorced spouse of the same person, still living, would not.

You are allowed to switch

This is the rule I most wish were printed on the front of the application.

The agency’s survivor amount page says that if you are eligible for a survivor benefit and another benefit, you choose the payment that is best for you, that the payments are not added together, and that you can switch benefits later. Its example is starting with survivor benefits and changing to retirement at 70, when that payment is highest.

The filing-rules page explains why this works. Deemed filing, the Chapter 12 rule that ties the two living-couple claims together, applies to retirement benefits and not to survivor benefits. A surviving spouse can start a survivor benefit independently of their own retirement benefit. The page gives an example of a 62-year-old widow who takes only the survivor benefit, leaves her own record alone to grow, and starts her own larger retirement benefit at 70.

So the sequence is a real choice, and it runs in more than one direction depending on which record is stronger. A survivor whose own record is modest may want the opposite order. The reductions apply to each benefit under its own rules and its own full retirement age, so ask the agency to price both sequences against your two dates before you file either one. Do not assume the order that worked for someone at your church is the order that works for you.

If you are working while receiving a survivor benefit, the agency’s amount page notes that earnings limits may apply depending on your age. Chapter 15 handles that mechanism in full.

The $255 and the two-year clock

There is a one-time payment, and it is small, and people are routinely startled by both facts.

The agency’s lump-sum death payment page states the amount as $255, payable to a spouse. If there is no spouse, the page says some children may be eligible: those 17 or younger, those 18 to 19 and in school full time through grade 12, and those of any age who developed a disability at 21 or younger. A spouse who did not live in the same home may still be eligible if they can get benefits on the record of the person who died.

The deadline is the part worth writing down. That page says you must apply for this payment within two years of the family member’s death.

Two years sounds like plenty until you have lived through the first one. Put it on a calendar the week you read this.

Since this comes up on the same phone call: the agency’s survivor amount page also notes you might get Medicare based on the deceased’s work history if you are 65 or older, or if you have a disability or end-stage renal disease. That is a separate program with its own enrollment deadlines, and it is outside this book.

Where a professional earns their fee

Most of this chapter is a phone call. Some of it is not.

Call the agency first, always, for eligibility and amounts. Nobody else can tell you what the record says.

Spend money on a lawyer when the relationship itself is the question. A divorce pending but not final at the death. A marriage performed in another country, an annulment, a common-law relationship, a contested second marriage, a decree whose effective date is unclear. Each of those asks what a document legally establishes, and the answer can turn on the law of the state where the worker lived when they died. Those rules vary by state. A family-law attorney licensed there can read the paper. Only the agency can decide whether it satisfies RS 00207.001.

Spend money on a tax professional or a fiduciary fee-only planner when the switching sequence runs into the rest of a widowed household’s income. Filing status on a tax return changes after a death, and the taxation rules in Chapter 16 do not care how fair that feels. The agency will not model your return. The sequence that produces the largest lifetime benefit is not always the one that leaves the most spendable money in a given year.

Nobody you pay can change a date on a decree or an entry in an earnings record.

Your survivor chart

Fill this in before you call, with your own numbers in the blanks. It takes about twenty minutes and it will make the call shorter.

  1. Write the deceased worker’s full name, Social Security number if you have it, date of birth and date of death. Missing the number is not fatal; the agency’s amount page says a representative will instead ask for details like the date of birth and the names of that person’s parents.
  2. Write your relationship: current spouse at the time of death, or divorced. If divorced, write the marriage date and the date the divorce became final, and apply Chapter 13’s ten-year count.
  3. If you were married less than nine months, write down any child of the worker, any adoption during the marriage, and the dates. Then ask the agency whether an exception to the nine-month rule applies.
  4. Write your own date of birth. Enter it in the tool described earlier in this chapter and write down the survivor age it returns. Label it “survivor FRA” so you never confuse it with the age from Chapter 10.
  5. Make a short column of ages from 60 through your survivor age. Beside each, write the percentage the agency’s amount page gives: 71.5 percent at 60, over 75 at 61, over 80 at 63, over 90 at 65, up to 100 at your survivor age. Mark the ages the page does not list as unknown rather than guessing between them. If instead you may qualify on disability grounds, start your column at 50 and leave every rate blank. Those figures are not published the way the age-60 scale is, so ask the agency for your entitlement date, any waiting period and the age-specific reduction that applies to you, rather than copying the examples above.
  6. Write whether you have remarried, and at what age. If the remarriage happened at or after 60, ask about the earlier record anyway. If it happened between 50 and 60 and a disability is involved, write down the date the disability began and the date any benefit entitlement began, and ask the agency to apply RS 00207.003 to those dates.
  7. Write your own retirement estimate at your own full retirement age and at 70, from your my Social Security account.
  8. Ask the agency for record-specific estimates in four places: a survivor benefit starting now, a survivor benefit at your survivor FRA, your own retirement benefit now or whenever you first become eligible, and your own retirement benefit at 70. Then ask them to compare both orders of claiming, month by month against your eligibility dates, before you file either one.
  9. Ask whether the limit in RS 00615.320 applies, including whether the worker was ever entitled to reduced retirement or reduced disability benefits. If it does, ask the agency for the applicable ceiling and your actual payable survivor amount.
  10. Ask about the $255 lump-sum payment on the same call, and write the two-year deadline on your calendar before you hang up.
  11. Write the date, the representative’s name and what they told you. If the answer depends on a document you have not sent, the answer is not final.

The hardest part of this chapter is that it asks you to do arithmetic in the worst month of your life. If you can, hand steps one through seven to someone who loves you and let them fill in the blanks. Then make the call yourself.

Chapter 15: Withheld Is Not Lost

He came to the Tuesday table at the library with a letter he had already read eleven times, and he put it down the way you put down something that has been biting you.

Early sixties. Still driving a route four days a week because the fifth day had been taken away from him, not because he wanted the time. He had filed for his benefit the year before, kept working, and then the letter arrived saying the agency would be holding back part of what he was owed.

“So that’s gone,” he said. “I paid in for forty years and they’re keeping it.”

I asked him to wait on the anger for twenty minutes.

Then I showed him the two sentences on the agency’s own page about receiving benefits while working. Beginning with the month you reach full retirement age, earnings no longer reduce your benefits, no matter how much you earn. And the agency will recalculate your benefit amount to give you credit for the months it reduced or withheld benefits because of your excess earnings.

He read it twice and said a word I will not print.

It was not relief, exactly. The money was still not in his account that year, and he had made plans around it. But the shape of the thing changed in front of him. I’ve seen people turn down work because they thought the withheld checks were gone for good.

Withheld and lost are different words, and the agency means the first one.

The test has an expiration date

The earnings test is temporary. Every explanation of it should start there.

The agency’s rulebook for its own staff, Program Operations Manual System section RS 02501.021, states that the test does not apply to people at or above full retirement age, and that this has been the case since January 2000. The public page says the same thing in plainer words: once that birthday month arrives, there is no limit on how much you can earn and still receive your benefits.

Not a higher limit. No limit.

So the whole of this chapter concerns the stretch between your filing date and the month you reach the full retirement age you found in Chapter 10. If you are already past that age, you can skip to the chapter on taxes, which is a different mechanism entirely and still applies to you.

And one note for the survivors reading this, because Chapter 14 left this question open on purpose. The agency states that if you receive survivor benefits, it uses your full retirement age for retirement benefits when applying the earnings test, even though your survivor full retirement age may be earlier. RS 02501.021 repeats it and adds that this holds even if you are not entitled to retirement benefits at all. Two ages, one of them controlling here, and it is not the survivor one. Of all the odd corners in this program, that one has cost people the most surprise.

Two limits, and which one is yours

Your expected earnings and FRA month determine which annual limit applies.

If you are under full retirement age for the entire year, the agency deducts one dollar from your benefit payments for every two dollars you earn above the annual limit. For 2026 that limit is $24,480.

If you reach full retirement age during the year, a different and much higher limit applies, and the deduction rate changes. For 2026 that limit is $65,160, the agency deducts one dollar for every three dollars above it, and it counts only your earnings up to the month before you reach full retirement age. Earnings in the month you turn that age, and after, do not count at all.

Both of those dollar figures are 2026 figures. The agency publishes next year’s each fall at ssa.gov/cola/, and Chapter 90 tells you how to go get the one that applies to your year before you act on any of this. Do not plan a 2028 work year around a number printed in this book.

The agency’s own worked examples on the receiving-benefits-while-working page are the clearest I have found, so I am going to use its numbers rather than invent mine.

In the first, you are under full retirement age all year, entitled to $800 a month, which is $9,600 for the year. You work and earn $33,400. That is $8,920 above the $24,480 limit. The agency reduces your benefits by $4,460, one dollar for every two over, and you receive $5,140 of the $9,600.

In the second, you reach full retirement age in August 2026, entitled to the same $800 a month. You earn $72,000 for the year, with $66,000 of it in the seven months from January through July. Only those seven months count, and they are $840 above the $65,160 limit. The reduction is $280, one dollar for every three. You receive $5,320 of the $5,600 due for those seven months. Beginning in August, the agency’s page says, you receive your full $800 per month no matter how much you earn.

Look at what the second example shows. The second example has higher annual earnings but only a $280 pre-full-retirement-age reduction, because its rules and counted months differ. The year you reach that age is a different country from the year before it.

Note too that both are separate hypothetical cases, and both assume the person is entitled to benefits for all twelve months of the year. If your benefits start mid-year, your own arithmetic has fewer months of benefits in it to withhold from.

What those published examples give you is the annual total. They do not tell you which months the agency will hold a check and which months it will pay one, and the mechanics of that are in the staff manual rather than on the public page. Ask the representative how the withholding will land across your calendar, because a household that budgets for twelve small checks and receives four missing ones has a problem the arithmetic did not show.

What counts, and the long list of what does not

More people are frightened by this test than are subject to it, and the reason is that they are counting the wrong money.

The agency is specific. When it figures how much to deduct, it counts the wages you make from your job, or your net profit if you are self-employed. It includes bonuses, commissions and vacation pay.

Then it names what it does not count: pensions, annuities, investment income, interest, veterans benefits, and other government or military retirement benefits.

Read that second list slowly if you have been dreading this chapter. A pension does not count. A required distribution from a retirement account is not a wage. Dividends, interest and capital gains are not wages. Rental income is not a wage for this purpose, though the agency treats some business activity as self-employment, so ask rather than assume. If your retirement income arrives without an employer attached to it, the earnings test very likely has nothing to measure.

Which leaves the people this chapter is actually for: those still drawing a paycheck or running a business.

For the self-employed, there is a second test that catches people off guard, and it is about hours rather than dollars. I will come to it in the next section, because it lives inside the first-year rule.

The rule for the year you stop

Somebody who works through June and files in July has a problem the annual limit creates by accident. They have already earned more than the yearly limit before their first check exists. Measured against the annual figure, they would lose benefits for months in which they earned nothing at all.

The agency wrote a rule for exactly this, and it is on the special earnings limit rule page. It lets the agency pay a full Social Security check for any whole month it considers you retired, regardless of your yearly earnings.

The monthly tests for 2026: if you will be under full retirement age for all of 2026, you are considered retired in any month your earnings are $2,040 or less and you did not perform substantial services in self-employment. If you reach full retirement age in 2026, that monthly figure is $5,430 under the same condition. Both are 2026 amounts, and both move with the annual update.

Here is the hours test I promised. The agency defines substantial services in self-employment as devoting more than 45 hours a month to the business, or between 15 and 45 hours to a business in a highly skilled occupation.

The page’s own example is worth repeating because it shows both halves working. A man retires from his job at 62 on June 30, 2026, having earned $37,000 before he retired. On October 5 he starts his own business, works at least 15 hours a week for the rest of the year, and earns another $3,000 after expenses, for $40,000 on the year. His annual earnings are far above the 2026 limit of $24,480. He still receives a benefit for July, August and September, because in each of those months he was not self-employed and his earnings were under the $2,040 monthly figure. He receives nothing for October, November and December, because he worked more than 45 hours a month in his business. Beginning in 2027, the page says, deductions go back to being based on his annual earnings limit alone.

Three paid months and three unpaid ones, in a year where a flat annual test would have taken a good deal more.

Now the part the public page leaves out. The staff manual, RS 02501.030, ties this rule to what it calls a grace year. Your initial grace year is the first taxable year containing a qualifying month, on or after the month your entitlement begins and before the month you reach full retirement age. That is not the same thing as the first year you were paid. If you worked hard through your first year or two of benefits and only cut back later, the grace year may be that later year. So ask whether this is your first qualifying monthly-test, or grace, year, even if you started benefits earlier. Raise your monthly earnings any year an unused grace year might still be sitting there.

The sentence I wish they printed on the letter

Now the part that sent the man at the library home in a different mood than he arrived in.

At full retirement age the agency recalculates, crediting back the months in which excess earnings cut or stopped what it paid you. The staff manual puts a name and a shape on this. RS 02501.021 says that months in work deduction convert to crediting months, that crediting months result in a higher monthly benefit, and that the higher benefit is realized at full retirement age. The companion section, RS 00615.482, grants a crediting month for any month of full or partial work deduction, and says a beneficiary needs only one crediting month to qualify for the automatic adjustment.

What that adjustment does is remove some or all of the reduction you took for claiming early, for the months you did not actually get paid.

Say that back to yourself in plain terms. You claimed at 62 and accepted a permanently smaller check, as Chapter 10 described, because the reduction is counted in months of benefits received. If the earnings test withheld your benefit for eight of those months, the agency goes back at full retirement age and treats you more like someone who received eight fewer months of early benefits. The ongoing check rises.

Before you plan around that larger check, look at what the recalculation won’t do.

It is not a refund. No lump sum arrives with the withheld dollars in it. What changes is the monthly amount going forward, from full retirement age onward, which means the value of it depends on how long you live to collect it. The staff manual also notes that cases with work deductions in the year you reach full retirement age carry a later review date, in May of the following year, so the adjustment is not always instant.

It is not dollar for dollar. The size of the increase depends on your own record and on how many months were withheld, and nobody can tell you the figure from a book. Ask the agency what the adjustment will do to your amount.

And it does not make the earnings test free. A withheld check in your sixties is money you did not have in your sixties, whatever arrives later.

There is a separate recalculation that people confuse with this one, and both can apply to the same person. Each year the agency reviews the records of all beneficiaries with wages reported for the previous year. If your latest year of earnings is one of your highest years, it recalculates your benefit and pays any increase you are due. That increase is retroactive to January of the year after you earned the money. So that one is about your earnings record getting better. The crediting-month adjustment is about months you were not paid. Different machinery, same direction.

Whose check gets hit

Your earnings are not always the only earnings in the calculation, and that surprises households.

The staff manual’s opening description of the earnings test says the agency uses it to measure the extent of a beneficiary’s retirement and determine the amount to deduct from the monthly benefits of the wage earner and auxiliaries. “Auxiliaries” means the family members drawing on that record. A worker who keeps earning can cut their own check and, on the same record, what is payable to a spouse or a child.

If you read Chapter 12 and built a household plan around a spousal benefit, bring that plan back to this page before you set a filing date.

There is a carve-out for former spouses that fits the pattern Chapter 13 established. RS 02501.021 states that the earnings test does not apply to divorced spouses on the basis of the wage earner’s excess earnings in two situations. One is where the wage earner was entitled to benefits before the month of divorce. The other is where the wage earner’s entitlement began in the month of divorce or later and the two have been divorced for at least two years. A divorced-spouse claimant’s own earnings can still reduce their own benefit. Their ex’s paycheck generally does not reach them under those conditions.

The manual lists other people the test does not reach, including those receiving disability benefits, with exceptions, and those working outside the United States in work Social Security does not cover. If either describes you, that is a question for a representative rather than for this chapter.

Where a professional earns their fee

Most of this is a phone call and a calculator.

Use the agency’s own Retirement Earnings Test Calculator before you call; the receiving-benefits-while-working page links straight to it. The calculator’s own note says the retirement earnings test always uses the normal retirement age applicable to retired workers, which is the same point the survivor paragraph above made.

Spend money on a tax professional or an enrolled agent when you are self-employed. Your net profit after expenses is the figure this test uses, and net profit is a number a return produces rather than a number you know in August. The hours question matters too, and it is less tidy than it looks. Even 15 to 45 hours in a highly skilled business can count as substantial; more than 45 usually does, subject to narrow exceptions the agency’s manual describes. One of those covers personal-service work where the monthly earnings are readily determinable and fall at or under the monthly figure. Log your hours and ask the agency to assess your particular work. Nobody there will keep your calendar for you.

And if you are weighing whether to work at all during these years, that is a cash-flow question, not a benefits question. A fee-only planner paid for an hour can model it. The thing not to do is take a smaller job out of a belief that the withheld money evaporates, because that belief is wrong, and it is expensive.

Your earnings test worksheet

Do this on paper before you file, or before January of a year you expect to earn well.

  1. Write the month and year you reach full retirement age, taken from Chapter 10, and beside it the month your benefits start or started. If you are claiming a survivor benefit, write that same retirement age here, not your survivor age, because that is the age this test uses.
  2. Write which case you are in for the coming year: under full retirement age for the whole year, reaching it during the year, or past it. If you are past it, stop. The test does not apply to you.
  3. Go to ssa.gov/cola/ and write down the earnings limit for the year in question and the matching monthly figure. Cross out the 2026 figures in this chapter and write yours beside them.
  4. Estimate your earnings for that calendar year: gross wages, bonuses, commissions and vacation pay, plus net self-employment profit after expenses. In a birthday-month year, count only what you will earn before that month. Then write your monthly benefit amount and count how many months of that year fall before your full retirement age month and after your benefits start. Multiply the two. This is your own pre-FRA benefit total, not necessarily the household maximum: if a spouse or child receives on your record, their payable benefits may also be affected. Treat the quotient as preliminary and have SSA calculate the record-wide withholding and monthly timing.
  5. List separately every dollar of income that is not in step 4: pension, annuity, interest, dividends, capital gains, veterans benefits, government or military retirement. Draw a line through the list. It does not count here.
  6. Subtract the limit from the step 4 earnings figure. Divide the excess by two in the under-age case, or by three in a birthday-month year. Call that your preliminary excess-earnings deduction. Do not cap it at your own benefit total if a spouse or child receives on your record; have SSA calculate the record-wide amount and monthly timing. Where step 7 applies, the monthly rule governs those months instead.
  7. If you are retiring or cutting back mid-year, write down each remaining month’s expected earnings and mark any month at or under the monthly figure from step 3. Those are the months to ask about under the special rule. Ask whether that year is a grace year for you, whatever year your benefits began. If you are self-employed, write your hours per month beside each one.
  8. Ask the agency three things on one call: how much it expects to withhold for the year, which months it will withhold from, and what the adjustment at full retirement age is expected to do to your monthly amount.
  9. If a spouse or child receives benefits on your record, ask what your earnings do to their payments too.
  10. Note the call date, who you spoke to, and each answer. Then tell them promptly if your earnings estimate changes during the year, because an estimate you never corrected becomes an overpayment you have to give back.

The man with the letter kept driving his route. He told me the following spring that he had worked out roughly what the adjustment would be worth and had decided it was worth working for.

Go find out what your own year actually costs you before you turn down the hours.

Chapter 16: The Raise and the Bill

Put the benefit-increase notice beside the SSA-1099. The larger monthly amount is on one page. A year’s benefits are on the other.

It can feel as though one envelope gives you something and the other takes it back. But the SSA-1099 reports benefits; it does not decide how much of them is taxable. That answer needs the rest of your income and your filing status.

The notices belong beside each other, not because they use the same formula, but because you need both to work out what you can spend.

The cost-of-living adjustment changes the benefit. Federal income tax may change what you keep. Start with the adjustment.

What the adjustment actually measures

The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, isn’t a reward for another year’s work. Under the existing law, it follows a price-index formula rather than a fresh vote each fall.

Social Security’s COLA explanation says the purpose is to protect benefits’ purchasing power against inflation. It uses the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, abbreviated CPI-W. The comparison runs from the third quarter of the last year a COLA was determined to the third quarter of the current year. The Bureau of Labor Statistics at the Department of Labor produces the index; the law names it as SSA’s measure.

That page also states the limit: if the index hasn’t increased under this comparison, there is no COLA.

Not a smaller adjustment. None. The agency’s own table of every automatic adjustment since 1975 shows 0.0 percent for January 2010, 0.0 percent for January 2011, and 0.0 percent for January 2016. Three years in recent memory with nothing added. The same table shows 8.7 percent for January 2023. All four results came from the same formula, which is the whole argument for understanding the formula rather than arguing about the result.

A short piece of history explains why it works this way. SSA’s history on the COLA page dates the provision to the Social Security Amendments of 1972; automatic increases began in 1975. Before that, benefit increases needed special legislation. A price index is a more useful planning basis than waiting for another bill. I’ll take the index.

The adjustment is 2.8 percent (2026). Social Security’s October 24, 2025 announcement gives that rate. Its latest-COLA page specifies December 2025 benefits, payable in January 2026. The December-benefit timing is not a typo; SSA says that has been the pattern after 1982. Increased Supplemental Security Income payments for January 2026 were scheduled for December 31, 2025, because January 1 is a holiday.

Chapter 10’s reduced benefit receives COLAs too. Applying an identical positive percentage to two different benefit amounts does not erase the difference: both rise, and their dollar gap grows. That is a comparison of benefit amounts with other factors held constant, not a prediction of two people’s bank deposits. Use your personalized notice for the amount SSA will actually pay.

Why next year’s number is not in this book

As of October 4, 2026, the COLA for 2027 has not been published.

That is not evasion. The comparison needs the completed third quarter’s price data, so SSA announces the result in October rather than at the start of the year being measured. Its COLA summary says the next announcement will be in October 2026. Don’t turn last year’s October 24 date into a promised date this year.

The annual information also includes Chapter 15’s earnings limits and the taxable maximum — the ceiling on earnings subject to Social Security payroll tax. Those figures are not the income thresholds for taxing your benefits. A page can contain several kinds of tax information without making them interchangeable.

So any book that prints a confident dollar figure for a year the government has not yet announced is printing a guess with a dollar sign in front of it.

Go to ssa.gov/cola and read the figure for the year you will actually be paid. SSA’s 2026 information scheduled online notices for late November 2025 and mailed notices for December 2025. Check the new year’s notice schedule rather than assuming those dates carry forward. You can choose available online notices in your my Social Security account. Chapter 90 gathers the annual checks.

Whether yours are taxed comes down to one comparison

Leave the COLA notice in place and pick up the SSA-1099.

The comparison needs two figures: half of your yearly benefits, and every other dollar of income on your return.

The second figure reaches well beyond a paycheck. IRS Publication 915, prepared jointly with SSA and the Railroad Retirement Board, supplies the federal benefit-tax worksheets. The edition available on October 4, 2026 is for 2025 returns. The examples and thresholds below are from that edition, not unpublished instructions for a 2027 return. Check the edition for your tax year before filing.

SSA’s tax FAQ calls the comparison figure “combined income”: adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest, and half your annual benefits. Use adjusted gross income before including any taxable Social Security benefits; don’t count them twice. Publication 915 supplies the required adjustments and add-backs for particular situations.

Tax-exempt interest. The municipal bond interest you were told was invisible to the IRS counts in this comparison. It is still exempt from tax itself. It still pushes the benefits calculation.

SSA’s withholding page uses the looser phrase “earned income.” Don’t read that as excluding a taxable pension, taxable retirement-account distribution or investment interest. Publication 915’s quick Worksheet A starts with half the benefits and all other taxable income, plus tax-exempt interest, without subtracting deductions. It is a screening calculation, not necessarily the adjusted figure the full worksheet will use.

On a joint return, include both spouses’ income and benefits. Publication 915 requires the other spouse’s income even if that spouse receives no Social Security. A worksheet containing only your own check cannot answer the joint-return question.

Let me put the base amounts on the board, from Publication 915 for 2025 returns.

For single, head-of-household or qualifying-surviving-spouse status, the base amount is $25,000 (2025 rules).

Married filing separately, but apart from your spouse throughout the entire tax year, also has a $25,000 base under the 2025 rules.

A joint return has a $32,000 base (2025 rules).

Married filing separately while living with your spouse at any time during the year has a $0 base (2025 rules). That case uses a different worksheet branch, with up to 85 percent of benefits taxable. Get help instead of using the individual tiers below.

For the other filing statuses just described, Publication 915 says generally up to 50 percent of benefits may be taxable above the base. Up to 85 percent may be taxable above $34,000, or $44,000 on a joint return (2025 rules). “Up to” matters: neither crossing a threshold nor multiplying the whole benefit by a percentage gives the actual taxable amount. The full worksheet does that.

The publication’s Worksheet A example for 2025 has a single filer over 65 with $1,500 of net benefits, a $17,000 taxable pension and $700 of taxable interest. There is no tax-exempt interest. Half the benefits is $750; the screening total is $18,450. Below the $25,000 base, none of those benefits is taxable under this example’s facts. Whether a return is otherwise required is a separate question for the current Form 1040 instructions.

Publication 915’s Worksheet 1 Example 1, also for 2025, shows a different single filer. A fully taxable pension of $18,600, part-time wages of $9,400 and taxable interest of $990 produce $28,990 of other income. Net benefits are $5,980. The completed worksheet gives $2,990 of taxable benefits.

These are separate IRS examples with different benefits and other income, not one person changing a single variable. They show why you need the whole year’s figures. Neither is an estimate of your tax bill.

Eighty-five percent is not a tax rate

Keep the word “included” beside that percentage.

Up to 85 percent of your benefits can be included in taxable income. That is not an 85 percent tax rate. The publication is explaining how much benefit income enters the return; the rest of the return determines the tax due, taking account of applicable rates, deductions and credits.

In the 2025 IRS example above, $2,990 is the taxable benefit amount, not the tax owed on the $5,980 payment. You haven’t finished the return when you reach that line.

I have watched people turn down a part-time job or delay a withdrawal on the strength of misreading that number. Understand what it says before you rearrange your year around it.

The numbers that never got a cost-of-living adjustment

The part I find hardest to defend is the mismatch: COLAs follow an index; the benefit-tax thresholds do not.

A later law could change the thresholds, but a positive COLA by itself does not.

Publication 915 makes the difference visible. Its Worksheet 2 covers lump sums for years after 1993 and uses the same $32,000 joint base and $25,000 individual-status base for those earlier years, with the separate $0-base married-filing-separately branch still distinguished. Worksheet 3 covers 1993 or earlier and has only the 50 percent calculation, not the later 85 percent tier.

Those are historical comparisons in the IRS worksheets, not annually inflation-adjusted thresholds. The higher inclusion tier applies to years after 1993; the publication’s 2025 base amounts still match the earlier-year amounts.

A positive COLA can raise your combined income even without another withdrawal or an extra shift. With the thresholds unchanged, that increase can move your own calculation across a line. It will not do so for everyone; your starting income and the rest of your return matter. I would rather the thresholds had an inflation adjustment too. They don’t acquire one just because the benefit does.

There is a newer wrinkle, and I am going to describe it carefully rather than confidently.

Public Law 119-21, enacted in 2025, changed federal taxes, credits and deductions; Publication 915 points to the IRS legislation updates. The IRS’s individual provisions page lists the official heading “Deduction for seniors (Section 70103).” A deduction can reduce taxable income without repealing the rules that include benefits in income. Publication 915 still prints the base amounts above for 2025 returns. Ask a preparer what the deduction does on your actual return rather than assuming that a headline abolished benefit taxation.

What the bank deposit leaves out

Chapter 15’s work-income test is separate from this broader combined-income tax calculation, which has no full-retirement-age exemption.

The income-related monthly adjustment amount, or IRMAA, is a Medicare premium adjustment rather than a tax on benefits; use Medicare.gov’s costs guidance and your determination letter for that separate question.

For the benefit-tax worksheet, Publication 915 says not to reduce box 5 net benefits by Medicare premiums or the other deductions it lists. Box 5 is the number it wants. A year’s bank deposits may be smaller, because money was deducted before it reached the account.

“Net benefits” on the form means box 3 benefits minus box 4 repayments. It does not mean what remained after Medicare and voluntary tax withholding. Use the form, not a total copied from twelve bank entries. If you receive multiple benefit statements, the publication tells you to combine the applicable box 5 amounts.

Withholding, and the form that does it

You have a choice about how the money leaves.

You can pay the IRS directly through estimated payments, or request federal tax withholding from the monthly benefit. SSA’s withholding page, checked October 4, 2026, offers 7, 10, 12 or 22 percent, not a freely chosen percentage. Start, change or stop a request in your my Social Security account, or call 1-800-772-1213. Publication 915 also names Form W-4V, Voluntary Withholding Request.

Withholding is a payment toward tax, not the final calculation. Publication 915 says to report the amount in box 6 of the SSA-1099 as tax already withheld on your return. Reconcile it with your other payments and your actual tax liability there. Don’t expect SSA to assess your whole return or automatically settle an overpayment of federal tax.

Ask a preparer whether benefit withholding, more withholding from another income source or estimated payments fits your year. Publication 915 directs readers to Publication 505 and Form 1040-ES instructions for payment requirements. December is a review point, not permission to postpone payments due earlier.

SSA’s tax-form page states that the 2025 form was available online February 1, 2026. Check that page for the next year’s availability rather than treating February 1 as a promise for every year. SSI payments aren’t taxable; if SSI is your only SSA payment, the agency doesn’t issue a tax form.

If the envelope never arrives, don’t wait on it. That same page offers the form as a download inside your my Social Security account and says most people also get a mailed copy. There is an automated phone route open 24 hours a day: call 1-800-772-1213 and, at the “How can I help you today?” prompt, say “ten ninety-nine.” If you live outside the United States and can’t reach the form online, the page sends you to a Federal Benefits Unit instead.

The widow’s return

Chapter 14 left one question for this chapter, and it is a cruel one.

A couple filing jointly compares against a base amount of $32,000. A surviving spouse filing as single, or as a qualifying surviving spouse, compares against $25,000, according to the base amounts in Publication 915.

Your filing status and income may both change after a death. I cannot tell you from here whether that makes more or less of your benefits taxable. Nor should you assume the return for the year of death must be single: establish the correct status first. The qualifying-surviving-spouse conditions are in the Form 1040 instructions, which Publication 915 tells you to consult.

If you are reading after a death, take the prior joint return, current benefit statements and revised income figures to a preparer while you can still arrange payments for the year. You shouldn’t have to guess at the filing status while also handling the rest of that household change.

What to pay someone to look at

Publication 915 explains which worksheet to use, including cases needing additional calculations. Its free Tax Counseling for the Elderly referral is a place to ask about pensions and retirement-related tax issues.

I would ask a tax professional or enrolled agent for help in the first benefit year, when you have a partial year’s checks but other income from the entire year. Separate married returns and the first return after a death deserve the same attention, because filing status affects the calculation. Don’t make a filing or withdrawal decision from this chapter alone.

A retroactive benefit payment covering earlier years is another reason to bring the statements and those years’ returns. Publication 915’s lump-sum election may lower the taxable portion by using the earlier years’ income. The taxable amount is still reported in the year you received the payment; the publication says not to amend earlier returns just to make this election. Chapter 17’s Fairness Act discussion can send you back here without rebuilding the tax rules.

Ask SSA about an incorrect benefit statement. Ask the IRS or a qualified tax adviser about how that statement fits your return. This chapter addresses federal tax; check your state revenue agency’s current instructions for any state return, rather than carrying these federal thresholds into it.

Your combined-income worksheet

Use this as a screening sheet when benefits start, then revisit it when income changes and in early December. It helps you know what to take to the official worksheets. It isn’t a completed tax return.

  1. Write the tax year, expected filing status and the Publication 915 edition you checked. If married filing separately with any time living with your spouse during that year, mark the special $0-base branch and take the figures to a preparer instead of using the general tiers.
  2. Total box 5 from all applicable benefit statements, or estimate annual net benefits for an unfinished year. On a joint return, include your spouse’s benefits too. Don’t subtract Medicare premiums or tax withholding. If the total is zero or negative, stop this estimate and follow Publication 915’s repayment instructions; don’t halve it as ordinary positive income.
  3. Divide the positive benefit total by two. Label it “half the benefits included on this return.”
  4. List other taxable income, using both spouses’ amounts for a joint return even if only one receives benefits. Use the taxable portion of pensions, annuities and retirement distributions, plus wages, net business income, taxable interest, dividends and other taxable income. For this quick screen, don’t subtract deductions or the exclusions Worksheet A says to add back. If you aren’t sure which portion is taxable, mark it unresolved.
  5. Enter tax-exempt interest separately, including your spouse’s on a joint return. Add it to step 3 and step 4’s total. Label the result “Worksheet A screening total,” not “tax owed.”
  6. Copy the applicable base from the tax-year publication. Under the verified 2025 rules, it is $25,000 for the individual statuses described above and $32,000 for a joint return. At or below that base, the quick screen shows no taxable benefits under its stated conditions. A missing income item means the screen isn’t finished.
  7. Above the base, complete the full worksheet the publication directs you to use, or have a preparer do it. It can account for adjustments the quick screen doesn’t subtract. Under the 2025 rules, the ordinary tiers have inclusion ceilings of 50 percent and, above $34,000 individual or $44,000 joint, 85 percent. Record the worksheet’s actual taxable-benefit amount, not just a ceiling. Special IRA-deduction or exclusion situations need the publication’s specified route.
  8. Keep unresolved items and any earlier-year lump-sum payment visible. Ask a preparer to compare a contemplated withdrawal or other income change against your whole return before you act. Crossing a line alone doesn’t tell you whether that decision is bad.
  9. Review tax already withheld from all income sources and any estimated payments. If benefit withholding is appropriate, choose one of SSA’s four permitted rates; otherwise ask what payment arrangement is needed. Note the action date and confirm the change. Don’t choose the largest rate merely because it is available.
  10. For next year’s benefit estimate, check the published COLA at ssa.gov/cola and your personal notice when available. Keep that annual update separate from your tax calculation; Chapter 90 carries the claim-file figure checks.
  11. Get the statement in hand before you start the arithmetic, using the account download or the automated phone route described earlier rather than waiting on the mail. Copy four figures onto this sheet in order: box 3 benefits paid, box 4 repayments, box 5 net benefits, box 6 federal tax withheld. Step 2 uses box 5 and step 9 uses box 6, so writing all four down once keeps a later question about a repayment from sending you back to the envelope. If you receive more than one statement, list each separately before combining.
  12. Mark which agency owns each line before you pick up the phone. SSA can correct a wrong benefit statement, change your withholding percentage and tell you what it paid you. It will not tell you how much of that is taxable. Its own withholding page states the comparison in rounder terms than the tax-year publication does, and prints the $25,000 and $32,000 figures with no year attached to them, which is reason enough to take your base amount from the publication instead. Send the taxable-amount question to the IRS or a preparer, and keep a dated source beside every number on this sheet.

Keep this year’s income sheet with the two notices. If the bank deposit and box 5 differ, you now know which number each question needs.

Set a reminder for the first week of December, and an earlier one if your income changes before then.

Chapter 17: The Rule That Finally Changed

Dolores taught twenty years in Ohio before she and her husband moved to Pennsylvania, and for most of that first career she paid into the Ohio teacher retirement system instead of Social Security. Later, in Pennsylvania, she worked long enough in jobs that did pay into Social Security to qualify for a benefit of her own. It was a small check. She assumed it was supposed to be small, because someone at a retirement seminar twenty years earlier had told her so, and she never checked again.

In the spring of 2025 a deposit covering past months landed in her account, and a letter followed telling her the monthly check was going up too. She called me before she called her bank. “Is this real,” she said, “or did somebody finally get smart about a scam.”

It was real. It was the Windfall Elimination Provision going away, and it was two decades late for her, through no fault of the rule’s own timeline. I’ll take the two decades up to a point: nobody should assume an old rule still applies to them in this one case. Check your own record.

What WEP and GPO used to do

Two separate provisions, two separate effects, both tied to the same cause: a pension earned in a job that never withheld Social Security tax. People call that “non-covered” employment. Teaching in many states, including Ohio, is the clearest example. Police and firefighter jobs in many municipalities are others. So are some federal jobs that predate 1984 and certain other state and local positions, depending on the state.

The Windfall Elimination Provision applied to your own retirement or disability benefit, the one built on your own earnings record. For some workers with a pension from non-covered employment, WEP lowered the benefit calculated on their own covered earnings. It did not reduce every such worker’s benefit; SSA’s old formula exempted workers with 30 or more years of substantial covered earnings. If you don’t know whether WEP ever reduced yours, check your SSA record before expecting an increase.

The Government Pension Offset applied to a different kind of benefit: a spousal or survivor benefit you were entitled to on someone else’s record, not your own. If you drew a government pension from non-covered work, GPO reduced that spousal or survivor amount, and it could reduce it to zero. This is the one that hit people the hardest, because a lot of retired teachers, firefighters and police officers expected the surviving-spouse benefit from Chapter 14 to be there, and GPO could take most or all of it.

The GPO was created in 1977 and revised in 1983; WEP followed in the early 1980s. Both were written into law to address a specific calculation problem in Social Security’s formula for people with mixed covered and non-covered earnings. Whether the fix was fair to any one household was argued for decades, in Congress and at kitchen tables like mine.

Both provisions sat on the books for roughly forty years, and plenty of households argued with them for the whole stretch.

What changed, in one sentence

The Social Security Fairness Act, signed into law in January 2025, struck both provisions from the statute entirely.

Not reduced. Erased. Going forward, a non-covered pension no longer lowers your own retirement or disability benefit under the old WEP formula, and it no longer lowers a spousal or survivor benefit under the old GPO offset. The calculation runs the way it would for someone who never had a non-covered pension at all.

That is the whole rule. The complicated part is what “going forward” meant for people who were already affected, and that is where the agency’s own rollout page matters more than anything I can print here.

Two kinds of relief, and why the second needs a record check

If WEP or GPO was reducing your benefit before the repeal, the law created two distinct results.

First, your ongoing monthly amount went up, recalculated without the WEP or GPO reduction.

For benefits payable January 2024 and later, the repeal removed the old WEP or GPO reduction. If SSA had already paid you a reduced benefit for covered months, it may have owed a retroactive payment for the difference while it updated your record. SSA’s Fairness Act page, last updated July 21, 2025, is the official place to check its current instructions and any case-specific exception.

That retroactive amount, if one is due you, is a one-time payment, separate from your new monthly amount. It is back pay for months already past, not an adjustment to future checks.

How many of those months apply to your household depends on your own record: when you were entitled, which provision reduced you, and what the agency already paid. That is a record question, and the answer sits in your file rather than in this book. If you call the agency’s general number, have your claim number ready and ask specifically about your WEP or GPO recalculation, not just “my check.”

Dolores’s retroactive payment arrived separately from her new, higher monthly amount, and the back pay came first. That matches the sequence SSA described in its February 25, 2025 announcement: most people would get their one-time retroactive payment by the end of March 2025, and the higher monthly amount would first be reflected in the April payment. SSA said in that same announcement that complex cases which could not be handled by automation would take longer, so your own sequence may have run differently.

You may be affected even if you assumed you weren’t

Here is the part I want you to sit with for a minute.

You do not have to be currently drawing a reduced benefit to be affected. You may be affected if:

You have a pension coming, or already draw one, from a non-covered job, even if you have not yet claimed either Social Security benefit.

You draw, or expect to draw, a non-covered pension yourself and are also entitled to a spousal or survivor benefit on someone else’s record. Read that twice, because people get it backwards: GPO cut your spousal or survivor payment because of your own non-covered pension, not your husband’s or wife’s. If the pension belongs to your spouse and not to you, GPO was never what shaped your spousal benefit, and the ordinary rules from Chapters 12 through 14 still govern it.

You assumed decades ago, correctly at the time, that WEP or GPO made a Social Security claim pointless for you, and never filed or never checked again. Dolores is the example. The rule that made her check small for twenty years is gone, and the smallness that was once correct is not correct anymore.

You are approaching retirement now, have mixed covered and non-covered earnings on your record, and were planning around a WEP-reduced estimate you got from an old my Social Security printout or a benefits counselor’s worksheet from before the repeal.

None of this requires a credential to check. It requires pulling up your own record and asking a direct question: does this still apply to me, given that the rule it was based on no longer exists.

What to actually do

Start at the pension. If either of you draws a non-covered pension, or expects one, then that person is the one whose earnings record and whose spousal or survivor eligibility need a fresh look, dated after the repeal rather than before it.

If such a pension is in the picture and nobody has rechecked the record since the repeal, do it now, in this order:

Check your current benefit estimate online rather than trusting an old printed one. If you are not yet drawing benefits, that figure should no longer carry the old reduction; if you are drawing a reduced benefit and believe it was caused by either repealed provision, that is exactly the case the recalculation is meant to fix.

Read SSA’s own update page, last updated July 21, 2025, start to finish, for who is affected, how the increase is figured, and how far back increased benefits may reach.

If your estimate or your payment still looks like it reflects the old reduction, call and ask specifically whether your case has been recalculated under the repeal. Note the date you called and who you spoke with.

If you have a non-covered pension of your own and you never filed for a spousal or survivor benefit on your husband’s, wife’s or late spouse’s record because you were told GPO would reduce it to zero, go back and ask again. Zero is not necessarily the answer anymore. If the non-covered pension belongs to your spouse instead, it is their record and their claim that need the recheck, and the call should come from them.

Choose the right route before you call

The next step depends on whether you receive a benefit, never applied, or cannot identify the pension’s coverage.

SSA’s current Pensions and work abroad won’t reduce benefits page says WEP and GPO no longer apply to benefits payable from January 2024. SSA will restore affected monthly amounts and repay amounts withheld since then; an unfiled claimant’s benefit is not reduced by the old provisions. That does not mean every pension holder qualifies for a benefit.

If you already receive a benefit

Start with any SSA notice about the change and the benefit information in your my Social Security account, which also shows your Statement and earnings history. Keep those with any older award letter or estimate showing a WEP or GPO reduction. You need to identify the affected record, not reconstruct the old formula.

Write down the benefit involved, notice date, and whether it describes a new monthly amount, retroactive amount, or both. Name any spouse or survivor claim separately; a change to your retirement record may not answer that question. Ask SSA: “Was this benefit reduced under WEP or GPO? Has this record been adjusted for benefits payable from January 2024? Is a retroactive amount due, and which months does your calculation cover?”

If notice and account disagree, record the date and answer when you call. Ask what would resolve the difference; a mismatch merits an explanation, not a conclusion that the law was misapplied.

If you never applied

An old estimate showing little or no payment after an offset is not a current eligibility decision. SSA says the old provisions no longer reduce benefits payable from January 2024, including for someone who has not applied. If you did not file because WEP or GPO seemed to make a claim pointless, ask SSA to assess the benefit now.

Keep eligibility separate from amount: “Do I meet the ordinary requirements?” and “Did the former offset affect this benefit?” Chapters 10-14 cover claiming rules. The repeal changes the offset, not eligibility; SSA decides what your record supports.

If the pension’s coverage is unclear

Do not decide from a job title alone; coverage can differ by employer and work period. Note the employer or public system, years worked, pension name, and whether the pension holder’s earnings history shows covered work. The account helps check earnings; the pension administrator can identify which employment supports the pension.

Bring those facts and any old SSA notice to the review. If work included both covered and non-covered jobs, say so rather than sorting the years into a formula. Keep documents available and follow SSA’s instructions about what to submit.

Before you contact the agency, make a short chronology for the person whose benefit may have been affected: when the non-covered job ended, when the pension began or is expected to begin, when the Social Security claim started, and which older estimate or notice showed the reduction. Keep the pension statement and earnings history nearby so you can answer a specific follow-up. SSA’s application guidance says to send supporting documents only when the agency asks for them; having a paper ready does not mean you should mail it unsolicited. If the person never filed, mark that clearly instead of writing a guessed benefit amount in the margin. The representative can tell you whether an application, a record correction, or a review of an existing award is the right next step. Write down that instruction before ending the call.

Keep copies of answers with the notice, not just a number on scrap paper; later correspondence may use a different description for the same benefit record.

If the person who received benefits has died

For a possible amount due on a deceased beneficiary’s record, SSA directs people to sign in and look for Form SSA-1724-F4, Claim for Amounts Due in the Case of a Deceased Beneficiary. It is distinct from the survivor-benefit application in Chapter 14. If both may apply, ask SSA which route fits each question.

Put the notice, account information, and pension facts on one sheet. Ask one record-specific question at a time; SSA can explain what it applied and what remains to be decided.

The tax question you’ll have, and where it already lives

A retroactive payment is income, and it can be a meaningfully sized check landing in one year instead of spread across the years it actually covers. Chapter 16 already gave you the tool for exactly this situation: the IRS’s lump-sum election, which can let you figure the taxable portion using the income from the years the payment actually covers instead of piling all of it onto this year’s return. I am not re-explaining the mechanics here. Pull Chapter 16’s worksheet and its professional-referral section back out, bring your Fairness Act retroactive-payment notice to whoever does your return, and let them run both ways before you assume the lump sum pushed you into a higher bracket than it actually did.

What this chapter does not cover

This chapter is the only place in this book that touches WEP or GPO, and it stays narrow on purpose.

It does not cover how to apply for Social Security retirement, spousal or survivor benefits in the first place; Chapters 10 through 14 already did that, and nothing about the repeal changes those filing rules.

It does not cover how your pension itself is taxed, how your pension plan’s own rules work, or whether you should take a lump sum or an annuity from that pension. That is a conversation for whoever administers your pension and, again, a tax professional for your own return.

It does not cover Medicare premiums, except for one narrow case. If your Medicare Part B premium was ever deducted directly from a Civil Service Retirement System annuity, or paid straight to the government because your check was too small or nonexistent under the old GPO reduction, a changed benefit amount can change how that premium gets paid. SSA’s update page addresses that specific situation in its own section. Medicare Made Plain owns everything else about Medicare premiums and enrollment, and I am not reopening that book here.

A straight answer about what I don’t know

I don’t know, sitting here, exactly how many months of retroactive payment your household is owed, how your own case stands by the time you read this, or whether a future law changes any of this again. Nobody writing a book in 2026 can promise you a 2027 implementation status, and I would not trust a book that claimed to know one for certain.

What I can tell you is that the rule Dolores spent twenty years believing in is gone, and the only way to find out if that matters to you is to go check, not to assume either way.

Could this affect me: a checklist

Work through this with your own documents, not from memory.

  1. Did you, personally, ever work in a job that did not withhold Social Security tax from your pay? Teaching, police, firefighting and some state, local or pre-1984 federal jobs are the common examples, but it depends on your specific employer and state, not the job title alone.
  2. Do you, or will you, receive a pension based on that work?
  3. If you answered yes to 2: could you also claim as a spouse or widow or widower on someone else’s earnings record? Your own non-covered pension paired with that second claim is what GPO used to cut.
  4. If you answered yes to 1 and 2: compare your current benefit estimate against any old estimate or statement you have from before 2025. Note the difference.
  5. If you answered yes to 3: ask specifically about that spousal or survivor benefit, even if you were told years ago that you did not qualify or would qualify for nothing. If instead it is your spouse who holds the non-covered pension and you do not, run questions 1 through 3 again for them, on their record.
  6. Reread the agency’s Fairness Act page before you act on anything here, and note the date it carries at the top; the July 21, 2025 version is the one I worked from.
  7. If anything still looks like the old reduction, call and ask for your case to be reviewed, and write down the date and the name of whoever you spoke with.
  8. If you receive a retroactive payment, set it aside, don’t spend against an assumed after-tax amount, and bring the notice to a tax preparer along with Chapter 16’s worksheet before you file.

If nobody in your household answers yes to question 1, this chapter was not about you, and that’s fine. Turn to Chapter 90 and get the rest of your figures confirmed for the year you’ll actually file.

Chapter 90: The Week You File

The application is open on the screen. Beside the laptop sits a folder: a birth certificate in a plastic sleeve, a marriage license, last year’s W-2, a bank statement with the routing number highlighted in yellow.

Leave the folder shut.

That sentence surprises people, and it is the agency’s own instruction, not mine. This chapter is the short list of things worth checking in the days before you file, and most of them are not documents at all. They are a date, a handful of figures that change every year, and an account you may already own and have never opened.

The week has two jobs. Fix the month you want the money to start, and confirm the figures that move every year before that month arrives.

Send nothing until they ask

Social Security’s application page says that when you apply, the agency reviews your record and checks the benefits you may be eligible for. If it needs documents or more information, it will contact you. Then it says the part people skip: to avoid delays, only send documents if asked.

I have watched the opposite instinct cost people weeks. The envelope goes out with certified copies of everything, unasked, addressed to an office that did not request it and has no claim pending to attach it to.

Keep the folder closed unless SSA asks for a document or more information through a request you can verify. If it does, send exactly what it requests and keep a copy and date.

None of which means your paperwork is irrelevant. It means the paperwork proves facts, and the facts are what you need at hand. An exact marriage date matters whether or not anyone asks to see the certificate. You will be far better served by knowing your dates cold than by mailing a shoebox.

The account is the file

Everything else in this chapter assumes you can sign in at ssa.gov/myaccount. If you have been meaning to set that up since the opening pages of this book, this is the week.

Inside it is your earnings record, and the earnings record is the whole calculation. Social Security’s review-your-earnings page explains the plumbing: each year your employer reports what you earned so the agency can update your record, and if you work for yourself you report it directly. The same page gives a maintenance habit worth adopting whether you file this year or in six years. Check in August that last year’s amount posted correctly.

August, because by then the prior year has had time to land. Not the week you file, when a missing year turns into a scramble.

If you cannot use the online service, that page points to Form SSA-7004, the paper request for your Statement, which you fill out and mail to the address printed on the form. Slower. Still better than guessing.

Use your account to check notices and claim status. For any notice, follow the delivery method and timing SSA shows for your account.

Let me put it on the board

Three annual figures sit behind the chapters you just read, and all three live on one page: ssa.gov/cola.

One. The cost-of-living percentage for the coming year.

Two. The two earnings limits that apply before full retirement age, which decide whether working costs you anything in the months before that birthday.

Three. The ceiling on how much of a year’s wages the Social Security tax reaches, which matters to you only if you are still earning near it.

This book used the 2026 figures, labeled as 2026 every time they appear, because those were the published amounts when it was written. Chapter 16 explains why that page changes when it does, and I am not going to explain it twice. What I want from you is narrower: open the page in the week you file, find the year you will actually be paid in, and write those amounts down beside the book’s.

If the page still shows the year that is ending, the honest note is the date you looked and the words “not yet posted.” Then look again. A blank with a date on it is worth more than a number you talked yourself into.

One more page belongs in the same sitting if a pension from non-covered work figures in your household. Social Security’s Fairness Act update carries a revision date at the top, and the version I worked from was dated July 21, 2025. The page also offers a subscription link, which is a reasonable thing to click if you are waiting on a recalculation. Chapter 17 covers what the repeal did; this is only the reminder to check whether the page has moved since I read it.

Pick a month, not an age

The application does not ask how old you feel. It asks which month you want benefits to begin.

Social Security’s timing page states the two mechanics plainly. You choose an enrollment month in the application, and your first payment arrives the month after the one you chose. You can apply up to four months before that month. The agency’s retirement-application FAQ, dated April 24, 2024, says the same four months.

So the decision you spent nine chapters making turns into one line on a form, and the line is a month and a year. Copy it from your worksheet rather than from memory.

The letter telling you whether you are approved runs on its own clock. The application page says that if you apply early, meaning two to four months before your chosen start month, expect that letter toward the end of the start month you picked. Apply closer in, and it typically comes within thirty days of applying. Either way you can check where your claim stands from the same account.

The day of the month your payment lands is a separate matter again, set by your birth date and the kind of benefit you receive. Your account shows the schedule. The agency’s automated line will also read it to you if you call 1-800-772-1213 and say “check delivery” when it asks what you need.

What to have at your elbow

Not documents. Facts, in a form you can read off without hunting.

Your bank’s routing number and your account number, because payments go to an account. Social Security’s direct deposit page handles changes through the account, and mentions a second route: your bank can transmit the information for you through a process called Automated Enrollment, though not every bank offers it, so ask yours first. If you have no account at all, that page points to the FDIC’s own guidance on opening one.

The month you chose, written as a month and a year.

Your own estimate at that month, taken from your record rather than from any table in this book.

If you expect to keep working, the figure you would actually bet on for this year’s earnings, and for next year’s. Chapter 15 explains what that figure does and does not cost you. Here it matters because the agency will ask for it and will hold you to it later.

If a marriage or a divorce bears on your claim, the exact dates. Chapter 13 explains how carefully those are counted. The application is not the place to discover you were off by two months.

And a way to reach a person, if you would rather not do this alone on a screen. The same application page lists the alternative. Call 1-800-772-1213 on a weekday between 8 a.m. and 7 p.m. Say you want an appointment to apply. They will book it and decide whether it happens by phone or in an office. The TTY line is 1-800-325-0778.

What you owe them after the first check

Filing is not the end of the correspondence, and the obligations that follow are the kind people forget until an overpayment letter arrives.

Social Security’s reporting page for retirement beneficiaries is short and worth reading once. If you said you would keep working when you applied, the agency sends you a form each year asking you to estimate your earnings. You are expected to speak up between those forms in two situations: when you expect to earn more than you estimated, and when you start working after telling them you would not.

The same page lists the personal changes to keep current. Your direct deposit account. Your contact information. Your citizenship or immigration status. Most of that you can do from the account; there is also a written route through Form SSA-795, uploaded with a brief explanation of what changed and the date it changed.

Then there are the life events. The reminders printed alongside the annual cost-of-living notice ask you to tell the agency if you marry, if you divorce, or if a spouse or ex-spouse dies, and to say so if a child receiving benefits on your record stops living with you. Chapters 12 through 14 are the reason those events matter to the money. Report these changes promptly; do not assume a record match, another agency, or another person will update your claim correctly or soon enough. Some of those events can open a benefit you did not previously qualify for as easily as they can close one, which is why the notice points readers to the agency’s own page on potential entitlement.

Report the change promptly using SSA’s current instructions, and record the date and method you used. A correction made late is a correction made out of your next several checks.

Nobody from the government wants a gift card

The cost-of-living page carries a warning I would rather repeat than leave out, because the weeks around a claim are exactly when people get targeted.

The agency states that its services are free, and that no government agency or reputable company will ask you for personal information or demand advance fees by wire transfer or gift card. It asks you not to hand over personal details, click strange links, or open attachments from senders you do not know.

Add my own rule to that. Do not give personal information or money to an unsolicited caller. End the call and use the number on SSA.gov or in your own account to verify any claimed SSA contact.

Suspected fraud goes to the Office of the Inspector General, through its reporting page or the hotline at 1-800-269-0271.

Your claim-file checklist

Work through this in one sitting during the week you plan to file. Write the date beside every line you complete, because in three months you will want to know when you checked a thing, not just that you did.

  1. Sign in to your my Social Security account, or create one. If sign-in fails, solve that before anything else on this list.
  2. Read your earnings history line by line, not just the total. Note any year that is blank, low, or filed under a former name. Date checked: ______.
  3. Open ssa.gov/cola and write down the cost-of-living percentage for the year you will be paid in. If the year you need is not posted yet, write “not yet posted” plus today’s date and set a reminder to look again.
  4. From the same page, write both earnings limits for that year, unless you reached full retirement age before January. Those limits stop mattering once you are past it.
  5. From the same page, note the wage ceiling the Social Security tax reaches. Skip this line unless your pay is close to that figure.
  6. If anyone in the household has a pension from work that did not pay into Social Security, open the Fairness Act update page and write the revision date printed at the top. Compare it to July 21, 2025, the version this book used.
  7. Write the month and year you want benefits to begin. One line. Copy it from your worksheet.
  8. Count backward four months from that month and write the earliest date you may apply.
  9. Write your own benefit estimate for that start month, taken from your record.
  10. If you will be working, write your honest earnings estimate for this year and for next year.
  11. Write the two banking figures from the section above. Confirm the account is open and in your name.
  12. If a marriage or divorce bears on your claim, write both exact dates as they appear on the documents, not as you remember them.
  13. Decide how you will file: online, or by calling 1-800-772-1213 for an appointment. Write the choice and, if you call, the appointment date and the name of whoever booked it.
  14. After you file, write the date you applied and the date the decision letter is due by the timing rules above. If it has not arrived by then, check your claim status before you call.

Fourteen lines, one afternoon, and the folder on the table still has not been opened.

Keep the sheet. When the first payment lands and the amount is not quite what you expected, this page is how you will tell a rule you misread from a figure that changed on you.

Then open the account one more time and confirm the start month you chose is the start month on file. If the start month is wrong, contact SSA promptly and ask what correction options remain.

What I Can’t Put on the Board

Somewhere behind you in this book there is a page in your own handwriting. Three dates in a column, probably, with one of them circled harder than the other two.

Nothing has happened yet.
