That isn’t a scolding. It’s the part people lose track of. A filled-in worksheet is a rehearsal, and a rehearsal costs nothing. The decision happens on a form, in a named month, and until you submit that form every figure you wrote down is still a draft you can tear up for free.

So let me spend the last pages on what changes the moment you stop rehearsing.

The door closes slowly, and it does close

A claiming date is not quite irreversible. It is close enough to irreversible that I want you to treat it that way, and I’d rather hand you the two real exceptions than let you imagine a more generous one.

The first is withdrawal. Social Security’s page on cancelling an application says you can cancel or withdraw your application up to 12 months after your benefit approval, that you can only do it once, and that you can reapply later. The form is Form SSA-521, the Request for Withdrawal of Application, which you can submit through your account or mail to your local office.

Read the price before you read that as a safety net. The same page says that if payments have already started, you have to repay the money you and your family received, plus the money the agency withheld for Medicare premiums, taxes and garnishments. If Medicare Part A covered any medical expenses during that stretch, those get repaid to Medicare too.

So withdrawal is not an undo button. It is a reversal that requires you to produce, in one piece, money that has already been spent across however many months. Full repayment can be difficult once a household has used the checks for living expenses.

The second exception only opens at full retirement age. The agency’s page on suspending benefit payments says that if you have reached full retirement age but are not yet 70, you can ask it to suspend your payments, and that you earn delayed retirement credits for each month they stay suspended. The suspension begins the month after you ask. If you never say another word about it, payments automatically restart the month you turn 70.

Two details on that page are worth more than the headline. You do not have to put the request in writing or sign it; the agency says you may ask orally or in writing. And suspension reaches further than your own deposit. If other people draw benefits on your record, they cannot be paid for the same months yours are suspended, with the narrow exception Chapter 13 covers. Any benefit you receive on somebody else’s record stops too. Your Part B premiums can no longer come out of a payment that isn’t arriving, so the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services bills you directly, and the agency warns that not paying those bills on time can cost you Part B coverage. If you also receive Supplemental Security Income, suspending retirement benefits makes you ineligible for it.

That is the whole set. A one-time withdrawal with full repayment inside the first year, and a suspension you can only start once you have reached full retirement age. Neither one is a plan. Both are repairs, and repairs cost more than getting the date right the first time.

If you are seriously weighing either, that is an hour of a fee-only planner’s time and a call to the agency, in that order, before you sign anything.

The question nobody wants to do twice

Back at the start I asked you two questions and admitted the second one was the one people walk around. I’ll say plainly now which it was: what the survivor lives on.

It is the hardest arithmetic in this book because it isn’t arithmetic. You are being asked to pick a number while imagining a specific person at a specific kitchen table without you in it. Everything in me wants to handle that later. Later is usually the week after it stops being hypothetical, and by then the claiming dates are set.

Here is the only instruction I’ll give about it. Do it out loud, with the other person in the room, once. Not as a plan. As a sentence said aloud: if I go first, your check becomes roughly this, and if you go first, mine becomes roughly that. Chapter 14 tells you where those figures come from and which full retirement age governs them. Saying the two sentences takes four minutes. That conversation may change which claiming date the household chooses.

If one of you refuses to have that conversation, you have learned something useful about how the decision is going to go, and you should probably have it with a professional in the room.

What in here goes stale, and what doesn’t

I’ve been careful in this book to label the figures, and you should be careful about which parts of it you trust in three years.

Before filing, use Chapter 90 to confirm the current figures that apply to your claim.

What ages slowly is everything underneath. How a reduction is calculated against your full retirement age. Why a spousal amount is measured from the worker’s full-retirement-age figure rather than from the deposit that actually lands. The difference between a benefit withheld and a benefit lost. Those structures sat still through the years I was reading about them, and they will probably outlast this edition.

Congress can change any of it. It did, recently, when the Social Security Fairness Act repealed two pension-offset rules that a lot of retired teachers and police officers had been told to accept as permanent. I’d keep that in mind the next time somebody tells you a rule is settled forever. Rules are only as settled as the last session that touched them.

The thing to do before you put this down

Open your my Social Security account. If you never set one up when I asked in the opening pages, this is the moment the asking stops being polite.

Look at the actual estimate for the actual months you are considering. Not my illustrations. Not the figure a neighbor quoted at you with great confidence. Yours, calculated from the earnings record SSA uses for your estimate.

Then write down one month and one year on a piece of paper, and leave it somewhere you’ll see it for a week. If it still looks right on the seventh day, treat it as your draft filing date. Before filing, run the checks that apply to your household and confirm any unresolved rule with SSA.

If it doesn’t look right on the seventh day, that’s useful too. Go back to whichever chapter made you uneasy and read it again with your own numbers in your hand instead of mine.

I taught long enough to know what happens when somebody hands a class the answer instead of the method. They pass the test and they cannot do it again in April. So I’ve given you the method, and the pages where the agency keeps the current numbers, and my honest opinion in the places where I have one.

The date is yours. Pick it on purpose.
